articles.title: हेटौँडामा पर्यटन वर्षको बहारः ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । बाग्मती प्रदेशको राजधानी हेटौँडामा पर्यटन वर्ष–२०८३ लाई लक्षित गर्दै ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान सञ्चालन गरिएको छ । ‘जाऔँ हेटौंडा, रमाऔँ हेटौंडामा’ भन्ने मूल नारासहित मनाइन लागिएको पर्यटन वर्ष २०८३ को पहिलो र प्रमुख कार्यक्रमका रूपमा ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान अन्तर्गत सरसफाइ थालिएको हो ।

यो वर्ष बाग्मतीको प्रादेशिक राजधानीस्थित हेटौँडा उपमहानगरपालिकाले पर्यटन वर्ष–२०८३ मनाउँदैछ । पर्यटन वर्षको कार्यक्रम अन्तर्गत सून्य फोहोर अभियान सञ्चालन गरिएको छ । यहि अभियान अन्तर्गत शनिवार हातमा कुचो र बोरा बोकेर जनप्रतिनिधि, सुरक्षाकर्मी, टोल विकास संस्थाका पदाधिकारी र स्थानीयवासी सडकमा निस्किए । हेटौँडाका सडकदेखि टोलसम्म सरसफाइ गर्दै उनीहरूले ‘शून्य फोहोर हेटौँडा’ अभियान शुरु गरेका हुन् ।

फोहोर व्यवस्थापनलाई केवल सरसफाइ अभियानका रूपमा नभई पर्यटन, वातावरण संरक्षण र नागरिक संस्कृतिसँग जोडिएको दीर्घकालीन अभियानका रूपमा अघि बढाइने योजना उपमहानगरपालिकाको छ । उपमहानगरपालिकाले ‘जाऔँ हेटौंडा, रमाऔँ हेटौंडामा’ भन्ने मूल नारासहित मनाइने पर्यटन वर्ष २०८३ को पहिलो र प्रमुख कार्यक्रमका रूपमा ‘शून्य फोहोर’ अभियान अघि सारिएको हो ।

मुख्य तथा सहायक सडक, सार्वजनिक स्थल र पर्यटकीय क्षेत्रको सरसफाइसँगै वृक्षारोपण र सौन्दर्यीकरणलाई पनि अभियानको प्राथमिकतामा राखिएको छ । टोल विकास संस्था नगर समन्वय समितिको संयोजनमा सुरु भएको अभियान नगरका ३ सय ७७ वटै टोल विकास संस्थामा सुरु गरिएको छ । पर्यटन वर्षको अवसरमा सुरु गरिएको ‘शून्य फोहोर हेटौँडा’ अभियानले नगरको स्वच्छता र सौन्दर्य कायम राख्दै हेटौँडालाई पर्यटकीय गन्तव्यका रूपमा चिनाउन सहयोग पुग्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको दाबी छ ।

पर्यटन वर्ष–२०८३ मा हेटौँडामा आन्तरिक तथा बाह्य पर्यटकको संख्या बढाउने उपमहानगरपालिकाको लक्ष्य छ । पर्यटकलाई आकर्षित गर्न नयाँ गन्तव्यको प्रचारसँगै शहरको स्वच्छता, सौन्दर्य र व्यवस्थित वातावरणलाई पनि प्राथमिकतामा राखिएको छ ।

यही उद्देश्यले सुरु गरिएको यो अभियानलाई नगरका ३ सय ७७ वटै टोलसम्म विस्तार गरिँदैछ । टोल–टोलमा सरसफाइ र फोहोर व्यवस्थापनलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउँदै हेटौँडालाई स्वच्छ, सुन्दर र पर्यटकमैत्री शहरका रूपमा विकास गर्ने र पर्यटन वर्षमा बढीभन्दा बढी पर्यटक भित्र्याउने लक्ष्य लिइएको छ ।

articles.title: इन्सेन्टिभ वितरण नहुँदा सेवा ठप्प, मर्कामा सर्वसाधारण विरामी
articles.summary:
महोत्तरी । प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरमा सेवा लिन आउने नागरिक अनाहकमा पिडित बन्न पुगेका छन । मेडिकल सुपिरिटेंडेन्ट, अस्पताल संचालन तथा व्यस्थापन् समिति अध्यक्ष बिचको तालमेल समस्या र भिडियो एक्सरे गर्ने स्वास्थ्यकर्मीको बाकी इन्सेन्टिभ जस्ता आन्तरिक विवादका कारण सेवाग्राहीलाई मर्का परिरहेको छ ।

प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरमा अस्पतालमा भिडियो एक्सरे सेवा बन्द भएपछि बिरामीहरू निजी स्वास्थ्य संस्थामा महँगो शुल्क तिरेर सेवा लिन बाध्य छन् । अस्पताल प्रशासनले प्राविधिक कारणले सेवा वन्द रहेको सूचना टॉस गरि सेवा अवरुद्ध रहेको बताएको छ । तर भित्री कुरा भने भिडियो एक्सरे गर्ने चिकित्सकलाई इन्सेन्टिभ उपलब्ध नगराइएका कारण सो सेवा विगत दुई हप्ताभन्दा बढी समयदेखि वन्द रहेको छ ।

प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरका निमित्त कार्यालय प्रमुख डा.रवि श्रीवास्तवले इन्सेन्टिभकै समस्याको कारणले दुईहप्ताभन्दा बढी समयदेखि भिडियो एक्सरे सेवा सुचारू हुन नसकेको स्विकारे । आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२\०८३ मा चिकित्सकहरुलाई इन्सेन्टिभ नदिएका कारण सेवा वन्द गरेको बताउदै समस्या समाधानको पहल गरिरहेको निमित्त कार्यालय प्रमुख डा.रवि श्रीवास्तवको भनाइ छ ।

प्रादेशिक अस्पताल जलेश्वरका अस्पताल सञ्चालन तथा व्यवस्थापन समितिका अध्यक्ष रोहित प्रसाद ठाकुरले पनि काम गर्ने चिकित्सकहरुलाई इन्सेन्टिभ नदिएकै कारणले सेवा अवरुद्ध भएको बताए । उनले सेवा सुचारुको पहल गरिरहेको बताउदै अस्पताल व्यवस्थापन समितिको जेठ २८ गते बसेको बैठकले इन्सेन्टिभ दिने निर्णय गरेपनि सो किन वितरण गरिएन ? आशंका छन् ।

स्वास्थ सेवा जस्तो संवेदनशील संस्थाले अस्पतालको आन्तरिक तथा प्रशासनिक समस्याकै कारण सेवा ठप्प पार्नु, आम नागरिकलाई अनाहकमा समस्या दिनु स्वभाविक रुपमा लिन सकिदैन्। तर, यसको समाधान कसरी होला? सर्वसाधारणले नै सोध्न थालेका छन् ।

articles.title: देश धान्ने क्षेत्रमै संकट, श्रमिक विदेश पठाउन बन्द !
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । वैदेशिक रोजगारीबाट आउने रेमिट्यान्सले देशको अर्थतन्त्र धान्न सहयोग पु¥याइरहेका म्यानपावर व्यवसायीले सरकारविरुद्ध दबाब बढाएका छन् । १५ बुँदे माग अघि सार्दै नेपाल वैदेशिक रोजगार व्यवसायी संघले शुक्रवारदेखि वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा श्रमिक पठाउने सम्पूर्ण प्रक्रिया बन्द गर्ने घोषणा गरेको छ । व्यवसायीहरूले नीतिगत सुधार नभएसम्म कामदार नपठाउने अडान लिएका छन् ।

नेपाल वैदेशिक रोजगार व्यवसायी संघले वैदेशिक रोजगार क्षेत्रका नीतिगत समस्या समाधान नभएको भन्दै शुक्रवारदेखि श्रमिक विदेश पठाउने कार्य पूर्ण रूपमा स्थगित गरेको छ । काठमाडौँमा पत्रकार सम्मेलन गर्दै संघले रेमिट्यान्सले मुलुकको अर्थतन्त्रमा ठूलो योगदान पु¥याए पनि सरकारले समयानुकूल नीति सुधार नगर्दा व्यवसायी र श्रमिक दुवै प्रभावित भएको जनाएको छ ।

संघले वैदेशिक रोजगार ऐन–२०६४ लाई समयसापेक्ष संशोधन, पारदर्शी लागत निर्धारण, वैज्ञानिक सेवा शुल्क, श्रमिक लक्षित गन्तव्य मुलुकको हवाई भाडा घटाउने तथा कृत्रिम अभाव अन्त्य गर्न माग गरेको छ । युरोपका नयाँ श्रम बजार, दक्षिण कोरियाको ई–सेभेन भिसा, जापानको ईएसडी कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन, महिला घरेलु कामदारका लागि नयाँ गन्तव्य खुला गर्ने र विभिन्न मुलुकमा देखिएका प्रशासनिक तथा बिचौलिया समस्या कूटनीतिक पहलमार्फत समाधान गर्नुपर्ने माग पनि अघि सारिएको छ ।

संघले मागपत्र प्रमाणीकरण र श्रम स्वीकृतिलाई पूर्ण रूपमा स्वचालित बनाउन, ५ हजारभन्दा बढी नेपाली श्रमिक रहेका मुलुकमा श्रम सहचारी तथा काउन्सिलर नियुक्त गर्न, व्यवसायीले राखेको धरौटीको ब्याज उपलब्ध गराउन र श्रमिकलाई बिना धितो सहुलियतपूर्ण कर्जा दिने व्यवस्था गर्न पनि सरकारसँग माग गरेको छ । अध्यक्ष खत्रीले विशेष परिस्थितिमा सरकारकै निर्णय कार्यान्वयन गर्दा व्यवसायीमाथि कारबाही गरिएको आरोप लगाउँदै अब नीतिगत सुधार नभएसम्म श्रमिक नपठाउने स्पष्ट चेतावनी दिएका छन् ।

संघले आफ्ना सबै माग सम्बोधन नभएसम्म शून्य समय घोषणा गर्दै वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा श्रमिक पठाउने सम्पूर्ण प्रक्रिया बन्द रहने जनाएको छ । व्यवसायीहरूको यो निर्णयले वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा जान तयारी गरिरहेका हजारौं नेपाली श्रमिक प्रत्यक्ष प्रभावित हुने देखिएको छ ।

articles.title: सेती नदि थुनिएर ताल बन्यो, स्थानीय जाग्राम बस्न बाध्य
articles.summary:
कास्की । केहि दिन यताको निरन्तर वर्षाले पोखराको रामघाटमा सेती नदी थुनिएर विशाल ताल बनेको छ । जसका कारण नदिसँगै जोडिएका सुकुम्बासी बस्ती बाढीले बगाउने जोखिममा रहेका छन् ।

सेती नदीलाई लिएर पोखराको भौगोलिक बनावट अत्यन्त जोखिममा रहेको चर्चा गरिन्छ , तर सेतिले निम्त्याएको जोखिम न्यून गर्न भने कुनै निकायको ध्यान पुग्न सकेको छैन । झट्ट हेर्दा यो दृश्य कुनै तालको होला भन्ने लाग्न सक्छ, तर नझुक्किनुस् यो कुनै ताल भने होइन ।

केहीदिन यता निरन्तर परेको वर्षको कारण सेती नदीमा पानीको बहाव निकै उच्च छ । हो पोखरा रामघाटमा फराकिलो रहेको सेती नदीको निकास सानो हुँदा पानी जान नसकेर विशाल ताल नै बनेको छ । सेती नदी थुनिएर ताल बन्दा अहिलेसम्म क्षति त भएको छैन तर संभावित क्षतिको जोखिम भने निकै बढेको छ ।

दाह संस्कारका लागि बनाइएका घाटहरु पुरै जलमग्न बनेका छन् । सेती किनारसँगै दुई दर्जन बढी सुकुम्बासी बस्ती छ, बर्खा लागे पछि कतिबेला बाढीले बगाउने हो भनेर जाग्राम बस्नु पर्ने अवस्था छ । अहिले ३ वर्ष यताकै ठूलो र डरलाग्दो तरिकाले सेती बढेको स्थानीय बताउँछन् ।

सेती नदी पोखराको अधिकांस भागमा भूमिगत भएर बगेको छ । पोखराको बीच भाग अर्थात् रामघाटमा भने सेती सतहमा देखिन्छ । यस आसपासको क्षेत्र अत्यन्त जोखिममा रहेपनि सुकुम्बासीका नाममा बस्ती बस्ने क्रम भने नरोकिदो जोखिम झनै बढ्दैछ । पछिल्लो समय झनझन गहिरिदै गएको सेती खोंच र निरन्तरको बर्षाका कारण कतिबेला ठूलो दुर्घटना निम्तिने भन्ने इतिहासविद्को चिन्ता छ ।

पोखराको भू–बनोट र निरन्तर वर्षाले भासिन सक्ने सम्भाव्यताले पोखरालाई वर्षेनी जोखिम तर्फ धकेलेको भूगोलविद्को बुझाई छ । नदी थुनिएर आफ्नो गतिमा जान नपाउँदा निरन्तर जमिनलाई खियाउनाले जोखिम बढेको भूगोलविद् कृष्ण प्रसाद पौडेल बताउँछन् ।

पोखराको भू–बनोट, बेलाबेलामा भएका जमीन भासिने घटना र भूमिगतरूपमा बगेको सेतीका कारण पोखराको जोखिमबारे बेलाबेला चर्चा हुने गर्दछ, तर त्यो चर्चालाई दीर्घकालीन समाधानको बाटोतर्फ भने कुनै निकायले लैजान सकेका छैनन् ।

articles.title: स्तनपान प्रवद्र्धनमा जोड, दोलखामा स्वास्थ्य सचेतना
articles.summary:
दोलखा । जीवनको दिगो सुरुवातका लागि स्तनपान प्रभावकारी कार्यहरूको सुदृढीकरण“ भन्ने नारासहित दोलखाको भीमेश्वर नगरपालिका–५ स्थित माटी स्वास्थ्य चौकीमा विश्व स्तनपान सप्ताह–२०२६ मनाइएको छ । कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमाहरूलाई स्वास्थ्य सेवा, पोषण सामग्री वितरण तथा महिला स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविकालाई प्रोत्साहन गरिएको छ ।

विश्व स्तनपान सप्ताह–२०२६ को अवसरमा दोलखामा आयोजित कार्यक्रममा धुलिखेल अस्पताल दोलखाका विशेषज्ञ चिकित्सकहरूले गर्भवती महिलाको स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण, अल्ट्रासाउन्ड, स्वास्थ्य परामर्श तथा स्तनपान र शिशु पोषणबारे अभिमुखीकरण गरेका छन् ।

कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमालाई पोषण सामग्री, ब्ल्यांकेट तथा महिला स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविका र माटी स्वास्थ्य चौकीका स्वास्थ्यकर्मीलाई छाता वितरण गरिएको छ । ती सामग्री पूर्व स्वास्थ्य चौकी प्रमुख रामकृष्ण मास्केको पहलमा विभिन्न दाताबाट संकलन गरिएको हो ।

कार्यक्रममा जिल्लाको स्वास्थ्य अवस्था, शिशु स्वास्थ्यमा आमाको दूधको महत्व र स्तनपान प्रवद्र्धन अभियानबारे जानकारी गराइएको छ । समुदायस्तरमा यस्ता कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिनुपर्नेमा जोड दिइएको छ ।

भीमेश्वर नगरपालिकाले मातृ तथा शिशु स्वास्थ्यलाई प्राथमिकतामा राख्दै स्वास्थ्य संस्थासँगको सहकार्यलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाउने जनाएको छ ।

नेपाल क्षयरोग निवारण संस्थाले समुदायमा स्वास्थ्य सचेतना अभिवृद्धिका कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिइने जनाएको छ ।

कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमाहरूलाई स्वास्थ्य सेवा, पोषण सामग्री वितरण तथा स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविका र स्वास्थ्यकर्मीलाई सम्मान गर्दै स्तनपानको महत्व समुदायसम्म पु¥याउने प्रयास गरिएको आयोजकले जनाएको छ ।

articles.title: भूपेन्द्रसहित बैंकका उच्च अधिकारीमाथि छानबिन शुरु
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । स्मार्ट टेलिकमको अर्बौं मूल्य बराबरको पूर्वाधार बिक्री प्रकरणले नेपालको दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रमा ल्याएको तरंगको पराकम्प अझै कम भएको छैन । लाइसेन्स रद्द भएपछि राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने सम्पत्ति चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँमा बिक्री भएको विषय अहिले अनुसन्धानको केन्द्रमा छ ।

सीआईबीले पूर्वअध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीसहित बैंकका उच्च अधिकारीमाथि छानबिन अघि बढाएको छ । नेपालको दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्र एउटा प्रश्नले अझै तरंगित छ । राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने स्मार्ट टेलिकमको अर्बौं रुपैयाँ बराबरको सम्पत्ति कसरी निजी हातमा पुग्यो ? यसको जवाफ अझै मिल्न सकेको छैन । नेपाल प्रहरीको केन्द्रीय अनुसन्धान ब्युरो अर्थात् सीआईबीले यही प्रकरणमा नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणका पूर्वअध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीलाई पक्राउ गरी अनुसन्धान अघि बढाइरहेको छ ।

काठमाडौं जिल्ला अदालतले भण्डारीमाथि थप अनुसन्धानका लागि प्रहरीलाई ६ दिनको म्याद दिएको छ । उनीमाथि ठगी, आपराधिक विश्वासघात र संगठित अपराधसम्बन्धी कसुरमा अनुसन्धान भइरहेको छ ।

स्मार्ट टेलिकमले २०७० सालमा आधारभूत टेलिफोन सेवा सञ्चालनको अनुमति पाएको थियो । तर कम्पनीले नवीकरण दस्तुर र रोयल्टीबापतको करिब ३० अर्ब रुपैयाँ सरकारलाई बुझाउन सकेन । त्यसपछि २०८० वैशाख ३ गते यसको लाइसेन्स स्वतः रद्द भयो ।

कानुनअनुसार लाइसेन्स रद्द भएको दूरसञ्चार कम्पनीको टावर, नेटवर्क, उपकरण र अन्य पूर्वाधार राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ । तर सीआईबीको आरोप छः राज्यको नाममा आइसकेको स्मार्ट टेलिकमको सम्पत्ति नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकले गैरकानुनी रूपमा लिलामी ग¥यो र त्यो सम्पत्ति एनसेल आजियाटा लिमिटेडले खरिद ग¥यो । स्मार्टको लिलामी मूल्य थियो चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँ ।

सीआईबीका अनुसार यो प्रक्रियामा तत्कालीन दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण अध्यक्ष भूपेन्द्र भण्डारीको भूमिका सबैभन्दा बढि शंकास्पद देखिएको छ । यही अनुसन्धानका क्रममा नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकका अध्यक्ष पृथ्वीबहादुर पाण्डेसहित ६ जना सञ्चालकको बैंक खाता रोक्का गरिएको छ । प्रहरीले उनीहरूविरुद्ध पक्राउ पुर्जीसमेत लिएको बताइएको छ ।

खाता रोक्का भएका व्यक्तिमा अध्यक्ष पाण्डेसँगै प्रणय राजभण्डारी, दीपांकर शाक्य, कविकुमार तिव्रेवाला, शालिकराम बेलवासे र शोभा श्रेष्ठ रहेका छन् ।

अर्का सञ्चालक मदनकुमार आचार्यले भने सीआईबीमा उपस्थित भएर बयान दिइसकेका कारण पक्राउ पुर्जीबाट बाहिर रहेको बुझिएको छ ।

फेरि एकपटक बिक्रि प्रक्रियाको कुरा गरौँ

स्मार्ट टेलिकमकोे सम्पत्ति बिक्री प्रक्रिया नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकले स्मार्ट टेलिकमले सम्पत्ति बिक्रिका लागि बोलपत्र आह्वान गरेसँगै अघि बढेको थियो । यसमा तीन कम्पनी सहभागी भए । ट्रान्सगेट टेकले ४४ करोड ५० लाख रुपैयाँ, प्रोफेसनल बिजनेस नेटवर्कले ४२ करोड ५० लाख रुपैयाँ र एनसेल आजियाटाले चार अर्ब ६० करोड रुपैयाँको प्रस्ताव पेस ग¥यो ।

बैंकले सबैभन्दा बढी रकम प्रस्ताव गर्ने एनसेलको बोलपत्र स्वीकार ग¥यो । तर यी तीन कम्पनीले राखेको खरिद मूल्य प्रस्ताव नै शंकास्पद देखिन्छ । सेटिङमै तीन कम्पनी एकै व्यक्तिबाट परिचालित देखिन्छ । दुई कम्पनीको प्रस्तावभन्दा एनसेल आजियाटाको प्रस्ताव आकाश जमिन फरक छ ।

यो किनबेचमा बैंकको दाबी छ, उसले ऋण असुलीका लागि बैंक तथा वित्तीय संस्थासम्बन्धी ऐनको व्यवस्थाअनुसार धितो बिक्री गरेको हो । तर जुन सम्पत्ति राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आइसकेको थियो, त्यसलाई बैंकले बिक्री गर्ने अधिकार कसरी पायो भन्ने सीआईबीको प्रश्न छ ।

यसअघि सीआईबीले स्मार्ट टेलिकमका सञ्चालक सर्वेश जोशी र नेपाल इन्भेष्टमेन्ट मेगा बैंकका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत ज्योति प्रकाश पाण्डेलाई पनि पक्राउ गरी अनुसन्धान गरेको थियो । सीआईबीले केही महिनादेखि यो प्रकरणमाथि अध्ययन अनुसन्धान गरिरहेको छ ।

तत्कालिन मन्त्री शर्माको भूमिका !

भूपेन्द्र भण्डारी दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्ष बन्नुअघि तत्कालिन सञ्चारमन्त्री रेखा शर्माका सल्लाहकार थिए । शर्माको जोडबलमा भण्डारीलाई प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्षमा तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री पुष्पकमल दाहाल ‘प्रचण्ड’ नेतृत्वको सरकारले नियुक्त गरेको थियो । प्राधिकरण अध्यक्ष बन्नुअघि भण्डारी इन्टरग्रुप टेलिकम एसएल लिमिटेड र स्मार्ट मोबाइल बुरुन्डीको प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत भइसकेका व्यक्ति हुन् ।

उनले मरु डिजिटल वालेट चलाउने कम्पनी पेनेपमा अध्यक्षका रुपमा ५ वर्ष १० महिना काम गरेका थिए । कार्यकाल ७ महिना बाँकी छँदै प्राधिकरणका तत्कालीन अध्यक्ष पुरुषोत्तम खनालले तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री प्रचण्ड र तत्कालीन सञ्चारमन्त्री शर्माको दबाब खेप्न नसकेपछि २०८० पुस २४ गते राजीनामा दिएपछि भण्डारी दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रको नियामक प्राधिकरणको अध्यक्ष नियुक्त भएका थिए ।

वर्तमान सरकारले सार्वजनिक पदाधिकारीसम्बन्धी विशेष व्यवस्थाअन्तर्गत भण्डारीलाई पदबाट बर्खास्त गरेको हो । आलोचकहरूले भण्डारीको कार्यकालमा दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रका समस्या थप बढेको आरोप लगाएका छन् । स्मार्ट टेलिकमका टावर राख्न दिएका दुई सयभन्दा बढी घरधनीले समेत लामो समयदेखि भाडा नपाएको गुनासो गर्दै आएका छन् ।

सीआईबीको अनुसन्धानले राज्यको स्वामित्वमा आउनु पर्ने अर्बौ मूल्यको दूरसञ्चार पूर्वाधार कानूनी प्रक्रियाबाट बिक्रि भएको थियो कि मिलेमतोमा भन्ने प्रश्नको उत्तर खोजिरहेको छ । स्मार्ट टेलिकम प्रकरणको अन्तिम निष्कर्ष अनुसन्धान र अदालतको प्रक्रियाले तय गर्नेछ ।

articles.title: टुसा व्यापारमा कडाई, पोखरामा माग भन्दा कम आपूर्ति
articles.summary:
कास्की । साउन लागेसँगै पोखराको बजारमा पहाडी क्षेत्रमा पाइने औषधीय गुणयुक्त टुसाको कारोबार सुरु भएको छ । पोखरा घुम्न आउने पर्यटकका लागि टुसा लोकप्रिय कोसेली बन्दै गए पनि यस वर्ष उत्पादन र आपूर्ति घट्दा व्यापार पनि सुस्त बनेको छ ।

अन्नपूर्ण संरक्षण क्षेत्र आयोजनाले चोरी निकासी नियन्त्रण गरेसँगै बजारमा टुसाको उपलब्धता कम भएको जनाएको छ । पोखरा घुम्न आउने धेरैजसो आन्तरिक पर्यटक फर्किने बेला स्थानीय कोसेलीका रूपमा टुसा लैजान रुचाउँछन् ।

औषधीय गुणले भरिपूर्ण मानिने टुसाको तरकारी पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा झन् लोकप्रिय बन्दै गएको छ । अधिकांश टुसा पाइने क्षेत्र अन्नपूर्ण संरक्षण क्षेत्र आयोजना (एक्याप) अन्तर्गत पर्छन् । संरक्षणसँगै स्थानीयको आयआर्जनलाई समेत ध्यानमा राख्दै एक्यापले हरेक वर्ष साउन महिनाभर सर्वसाधारणलाई टुसा संकलन गर्न अनुमति दिने गरेको छ ।

असारदेखि भदौसम्म टुसा पलाउने मुख्य याम हो । कास्कीका ल्वाङ, घलेल, भुर्जुङखोला, सिक्लेस, ताङतिङ, याङजाकोट, घान्द्रुक, लान्द्रुक, धम्पुस र लुम्लेलगायत उच्च पहाडी क्षेत्रबाट बजारमा टुसा ल्याइन्छ । मानव स्वास्थ्यका लागि उपयोगी भएकाले यसको महत्व हरेक वर्ष बढ्दै गएको एक्यापको भनाइ छ ।

साउन महिनामा धेरैले माछामासु कम खाने परम्परा र यही समयमा टुसाको उत्पादन बढी हुने भएकाले व्यापार पनि बढ्ने गरेको थियो । तर यस वर्ष भने बजारको अवस्था फरक देखिएको छ । व्यापारीका अनुसार उत्पादन कम भएकाले बजारमा टुसाको आपूर्ति घटेको छ ।

अहिले पोखरामा प्रतिमुठा ८० देखि १५० रुपैयाँसम्ममा बिक्री भइरहेको छ । राम्रो व्यापार भएका दिन एकै स्थानबाट दुई सय मुठासम्म बिक्री हुने गरे पनि अघिल्लो वर्षको तुलनामा यसपालि कारोबार घटेको व्यवसायीको भनाइ छ ।

पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा टुसाको चोरी निकासी बढेपछि एक्यापले व्यवस्थापन कडा बनाएको छ । बोलकबोल प्रक्रियामार्फत वैधानिक रूपमा संकलन र बिक्रीको व्यवस्था गरिएको छ ।

अघिल्ला वर्षमा करिब ९ लाख टुसा निकासा गरिएकोमा यस वर्ष ६ लाख मात्रै निकासा गरिएको र चोरी निकासी नियन्त्रण गरिएकाले पनि बजारमा टुसाको उपलब्धता कम भएको एक्यापले जनाएको छ ।

उच्च पहाडी क्षेत्रको प्राकृतिक उत्पादन टुसा जडीबुटी मात्र होइन, पोखराको पहिचान बनेको कोसेली पनि हो । तर उत्पादनमा कमी र अवैध निकासी नियन्त्रणको प्रभाव यस वर्ष बजारमा स्पष्ट देखिएको छ ।

संरक्षण र व्यवस्थित व्यवस्थापनसँगै उत्पादन बढाउन सकिए टुसाको व्यापारले स्थानीय अर्थतन्त्रलाई अझ बलियो बनाउने अपेक्षा समेत गरिएको छ ।

articles.title: महारथीको सम्मान लिन नेपाल आउँदै जनरल सेठ
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्धको पुरानो परम्परालाई निरन्तरता दिन भारतीय स्थल सेनाप्रमुख जनरल धीरज सेठ साउन ३१ गते नेपाल भ्रमणमा आउँदैछन् । मानार्थ महारथीको सम्मान पाउने जनरल सेठको यो भ्रमणसँगै गोर्खा भर्ती, अग्निपथ योजना र सीमामा नेपाली नागरिकमाथि हुने व्यवहारका विषय पनि चर्चामा छन् ।

भारतीय स्थल सेनाका प्रमुख जनरल धीरज सेठ पाँच दिने औपचारिक भ्रमणका लागि साउन ३१ गते अर्थात् अगस्ट १६ मा नेपाल आउँदैछन् । नेपाली सेनाका प्रधानसेनापति अशोकराज सिग्देलको निमन्त्रणामा हुन लागेको यो भ्रमणलाई नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्धको निरन्तरताका रूपमा हेरिएको छ ।

भ्रमणका क्रममा जनरल सेठलाई नेपाली सेनाको मानार्थ महारथी दर्जाको दज्र्यानी चिह्न प्रदान गरिने कार्यक्रम छ । सन् १९५० देखि नेपाल र भारतले एकअर्काका सेना प्रमुखलाई मानार्थ महारथीको सम्मान प्रदान गर्दै आएका छन् । यो परम्परालाई दुई देशबीचको विश्वास, मित्रता र सैनिक सहकार्यको एउटा विशिष्ट प्रतिक मानिएको छ ।

यसअघि २०८१ मंसिर २७ गते नेपाली सेनाका प्रधानसेनापति अशोकराज सिग्देललाई भारतको नयाँदिल्लीमा आयोजित विशेष समारोहमा भारतीय राष्ट्रपति द्रौपदी मुर्मुले भारतीय सेनाको मानार्थ महारथीको दज्र्यानी चिह्न प्रदान गरेकी थिइन् ।

नेपाल–भारत सैनिक सम्बन्ध !

नेपाल र भारतबीचको सैनिक सम्बन्ध शताब्दीयौँ पुरानो मानिन्छ । स्वतन्त्र भारत र नेपालबीच सन् १९५० को शान्ति तथा मैत्री सन्धिपछि दुई देशबीचको रक्षा सहकार्य अझ संस्थागत बनेको हो । दुवै देशका सेनाले संयुक्त सैन्य अभ्यास सूर्य किरण, विपद् व्यवस्थापन, सीमा सुरक्षासम्बन्धी समन्वय, तालिम आदान–प्रदान तथा उच्च तहका भ्रमणलाई निरन्तरता दिँदै आएका छन् ।

यस्तै नेपाली नागरिक भारतीय सेनामा भर्ती हुने व्यवस्था पनि दुई देशबीचको विशेष सम्बन्धको अर्को आधार हो ।

गोर्खा सैनिकका रूपमा नेपाली युवाले करिब दुई सय वर्षदेखि भारतीय सेनामा सेवा गर्दै आएका छन् । अहिले पनि हजारौँ नेपाली नागरिक भारतीय सेनाका विभिन्न गोर्खा रेजिमेन्टमा कार्यरत छन् भने ठूलो संख्यामा पूर्वगोर्खा सैनिकले पेन्सन र अन्य सुविधा प्राप्त गरिरहेका छन् ।

अग्निपथले रोकिएको भर्ति !

तर पछिल्ला वर्षमा भारतीय सेनाको अग्निपथ योजना लागू भएपछि नेपाली नागरिकको भर्ती प्रक्रिया प्रभावित भएको छ । नेपाल सरकारले अग्निपथ योजनाबारे औपचारिक धारणा नटुंग्याएको भन्दै नेपाली युवाको भारतीय सेनामा नयाँ भर्ती रोकिएको अवस्था छ ।

चार वर्षे कार्यकाल र त्यसपछि २५ प्रतिशतलाई मात्रै नियमित सेवामा राखिने अग्गिपथ अन्तर्गतको मापदण्डका कारण लामो समयदेखि कायम रहेको गोर्खा भर्ती रोकिएको हो । यो विषयमा दुवै देशबीच कूटनीतिक तहमा छलफल हुँदै आएको छ ।

सीमा दुखेको सम्बन्ध !

नेपाली सेना र भारतीय सेनाबीच मानार्थ महारथीको विशिष्ट परम्परा रहँदा रहँदै पनि सीमामा भारतीय सीमा सुरक्षा बल एसएसबीले नेपाली नागरिकमाथि गर्ने दुव्र्यवहारका घटना बेलाबेला सार्वजनिक हुँदै आएका छन् ।

एसएसबीले सीमा क्षेत्रमा कुटपिट, अनावश्यक नियन्त्रण, गोली चलाइएका घटना तथा नेपाली नागरिकमाथि भएको दुव्र्यवहारले नेपाली नागरिकले अक्सर भारतसँग चित्त दुखाउनु परेको छ । यस्ता घटनापछि नेपाली पक्षबाट कूटनीतिक विरोध भएपनि दीर्घकालीन समाधान भने हुन सकेको छैन ।

articles.title: वित्तीय क्षेत्रको निष्पक्षता नै अर्थतन्त्रको मेरुदण्डः एक्यान अध्यक्ष नेपाल
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल चार्टर्ड एकाउण्टेण्ट्स संघ (एक्यान) का अध्यक्ष अनुप नेपालले वित्तीय क्षेत्रको निष्पक्षता नै अर्थतन्त्रको मेरुदण्ड भएको बताएका छन् ।

नेपाल अडिटर्स एसोसिएसन (अडान) को वार्षिक साधारण सभालाई सम्बोधन गर्दै उनले मुलुकको अर्थतन्त्रमा पारदर्शिता र वित्तीय सुशासन कायम गर्न लेखापरीक्षण क्षेत्रको भूमिका महत्वपूर्ण हुने बताए । उनले राज्यको राजस्व सङ्कलनलाई पारदर्शी बनाउन र व्यावसायिक क्षेत्रमा विश्वास अभिवृद्धि गर्न लेखापरीक्षकहरूले गरेको योगदानको प्रशंसा गरे ।

एक्यान र अडान दुवै संस्थाको साझा लक्ष्य नेपाली लेखा व्यवसायलाई थप मर्यादित, पारदर्शी र उत्तरदायी बनाउनु रहेको भन्दै उनले पेसागत हकहित र नीतिगत सुधारका लागि सहकार्य आवश्यक रहेको बताए ।

उनले आजको समय प्रविधिमैत्री युग रहेको भन्दै यसमा पनि अडिटर्सहरुले आफूलाई प्रविधिमैत्री बनाउनुपर्नेमा जोड दिए । अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय लेखापरीक्षण मापदण्ड र कर प्रणालीका नयाँ चुनौतीहरूको सामना गर्नका दक्षता अभिवृद्धि गर्नुपर्ने उनको सुझाव छ । पछिल्लो समयको एआई प्रविधिहरुबाट कोही पनि आतंकित हुनु नपर्ने भन्दै प्रविधिलाई केवल एउटा साधनका रूपमा लिन उनले आग्रह गरे ।

उनले क्याल्कुलेटरको आविष्कारको उदाहरण दिँदै क्याकुलेटर आज सामान्य र आवश्यक भएजस्तै एआई जस्ता प्रविधिहरु आगामी दशकमा उस्तै अत्यावश्यक बन्ने बताए ।

खासगरी उच्च व्यावसायिक नैतिकता, निष्पक्षता र इमानदारितालाई आत्मसाथ गरि समाज र राज्यको लेखापरीक्षण पेशाप्रतिको विश्वासलाई मजबुत बनाउनुपर्नेमा उनले जोड दिएका छन् ।

articles.title: गुप्तचर निकायमाथि चौतर्फि आलोचना, संयन्त्रमाथि गम्भिर प्रश्न
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । सुनसरी घटनापछि राज्यको सुरक्षा संयन्त्रको मात्र होइन, राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान विभागको भूमिका र औचित्यमाथि नयाँ बहस शुरु भएको छ । राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान विभाग प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालय मातहत राख्ने कि गृहमन्त्रालय मातहत रहने भन्नेमा सांसदहरुबीच नै फरक फरक मत रहेका छन् । प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह पनि गुप्तचरी निकायको कामप्रति सन्तुष्ट हुन सकेका छैनन् ।

देशभित्र हुने भू–राजनीतिक चलखेल, वैदेशिक हस्तक्षेप, आन्तरिक अस्थिरता तथा आन्दोलनमा हुने घुसपैठको निगरानी गर्ने जिम्मेवारी बोकेको संस्था हो, राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान विभाग । तर प्रश्न उठ्छ के राअवि आफनो भूमिकामा प्रभावकारी छ ? पछिल्लो समय यसको प्रभावकारीता खस्कँदै गएको देखिन्छ । सरकारले पनि यसको भूमिका र महत्वप्रति आवश्यक चासो देखाउन छाडेको छ । संसदमा पनि अनुसन्धानको भूमिका माथि प्रश्नहरु उठाइएका छन् ।

नेपालमा किन गुप्तचर निकाय यति कमजोर बन्दै गएको छ ? दक्षिणी छिमेकी मुलुक भारतमा आन्तरिक सुरक्षाका लागि इन्टेलिजेन्स ब्यूरो आईबी र बाह्य रणनीतिक सूचनाका लागि रिसर्च एन्ड एनालाइसिस विंग ‘रअ’ छन् । यी सस्थाहरु कानुनी दायरा भित्र रहेर अत्यन्त शक्तिशाली रुपमा परिचालित छन । आबश्यक परेमा फोन ट्यापिङ समेत गर्न सक्ने अधिकार उनीहरुसँग छ । तर स्पष्ट कानुनी संरचना भित्र बसेर मात्र । भारतमा गुप्तचर प्रमुखहरू प्रधानमन्त्रीसँग प्रत्यक्ष संवाद गर्न सक्छन । तर नेपालमा गुप्तचर निकाय राअवि प्रधानमन्त्री मातहत रहेपनि प्रधानमन्त्रीसँग देशको सुरक्षा चुनौती बारे छलफल गर्न त परको कुरा सूचना संकलन गर्न समेत चुकेका छन् ।

अब लगौं केही घटना तर्फः साउन १० गते राति सुनसरीको कप्तानगन्जमा दुई समूहबीच विवाद सुरु हुँदा स्थानीय प्रहरी चौकीबाट खटिएको टोली नै आफैं आक्रमणमा पर्यो। स्थिति नियन्त्रण बाहिर गएपछि प्रहरी र सशस्त्रले दर्जनौँ राउन्ड हवाई फायर गर्नुप¥यो। तर प्रश्न यो उठ्छ— यति ठूलो साम्प्रदायिक तनावको पूर्वसूचना सुरक्षा निकाय र गुप्तचरले किन पाएन ?

गृहमन्त्रीले समेत घटनाअघि कुनै पनि निकायबाट पूर्वसूचना नआएको बताइसकेका छन्। सुनसरीमा अनुसन्धानका एसपी सरहका उपअनुसन्धान निर्देशक विमल घिमिरेको नेतृत्वमा टोली खटिएको थियो । प्रदेशमा डीआईजी सरहका अनुसन्धान निर्देशक इन्द्र लामा नेतृत्वको टोली खटिएको भए पनि उनीहरूले यसबारे सम्भावित द्वन्द्वको सुइँकोसमेत पाउन सकेन ।

सुनसरीमा स्थिति बिग्रिँदै गएपछि प्रधानमन्त्री वालेन्द्र शाहले नेपाल प्रहरीका प्रमुख दानबहादुर कार्की र सशस्त्र प्रहरी प्रमुख नारायणदत्त पौडेललाई प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालयमा बोलाएर घटनाको विस्तृत ब्रिफिङ लिएका थिए । तर, यति ठुलो घटना हुँदा पनि प्रधानमन्त्रीले आफू मातहत नै रहेको गुप्तचर निकाय राअविका प्रमुख टेकेन्द्र कार्कीलाई भने बैठकमा बोलाएनन् ।

यस्तो छ अनुसन्धान विभागको संरचना र जिम्मेवारी

मुलुकभर राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान विभागको संरचना छ । सिंहदरबार दक्षिण गेटसँगै विभागको मुख्यालय छ । विभागका २ हजार २६५ जना कर्मचारी र एजेन्टहरूलाई सूचना सङ्कलन गर्ने जिम्मेवारी दिइएको हुन्छ । जिल्ला इन्चार्ज र केन्द्रमा विभागीय प्रमुखले तोकेका एजेन्टहरूले पनि विभागलाई सूचना उपलब्ध गराउँछन् । मुख्य अनुसन्धान निर्देशकको नेतृत्वमा विभागमा दुई जना अतिरिक्त मुख्य अनुसन्धान निर्देशक हुन्छन् ।

९ जना अनुसन्धान निर्देशक छन् । अनुसन्धान निर्देशकहरू ७ वटा प्रदेश, उपत्यकामा र प्रशासन विभागमा छन् । सह–अनुसन्धान निर्देशक ११ जना छन् ।

काठमाडौँ, ललितपुर, त्रिभुवन अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय विमानस्थल र हेटौंडास्थित इन्टेलिजेन्स शिक्षालयमा सहअनुसन्धान निर्देशकले कमाण्ड गर्छन् । उपअनुसन्धान निर्देशक ५३ जना र प्रमुख अनुसन्धान अधिकृत ९० जना छन् । अनुसन्धान अधिकृतहरू १६० जना छन् ।

विभागलाई सरकारले २ अर्बभन्दा बढी बजेट विनियोजन गर्दे आएकोमा यसपालि भने ५० प्रतिशत कटौती गरिएको छ । कार्यप्रकृतिअनुसार राअविले देशको राष्ट्रिय सुरक्षामा असर पर्न सक्ने विषयमा सूचना संकलन गरेर घटना हुनुअगावै सरकारलाई जानकारी दिनुपर्ने हो । नेपाल प्रहरी र सशस्त्र प्रहरी घटना भइसकेपछि खटिने हुन्, अनुसन्धान जस्तो निकाय घटना हुनुअगावै परिचालित हुने हो । तर राअवि यही काममा पटक–पटक चुक्दै आएको छ, जसका कारण गुप्तचरका प्रतिवेदन र विश्लेषणलाई राजनीतिक नेतृत्वले प्राथमिकता दिन छाडेका छन ।

त्यसको असर गत बर्षको भदौ २३ मा भएको जेन–जी आन्दोलनमा देखिएको थियो,जति बेला राअविको एक साता अघिदेखिको प्रतिवेदन तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री केपी शर्मा ओलीले खोलेर हेरेकै थिएनन् । २०८१ चैत १५ गते तीनकुने क्षेत्रमा भएको दुर्गा प्रसाईं नेतृत्वको आन्दोलन तथा भदौ २३–२४ मा भएको जेन–जी आन्दोलनका क्रममा राज्य संयन्त्र पूर्वसूचना संकलनमा निकै कमजोर देखियो ।

आन्दोलनको स्वरूप, उद्देश्य तथा सहभागीबारे स्पष्ट जानकारी नहुँदा सुरक्षा निकायहरू आकस्मिक बल प्रयोग गर्नुपर्ने अवस्थामा पुगेका थिए ।

नेपाल दुई ठूला शक्ति भारत र चीनबीच रहेको संवेदनशील भूराजनीतिक अवस्थाको राष्ट्र हो । यस्तो अवस्थामा गुप्तचर संयन्त्र कमजोर हुँदा राष्ट्रिय सुरक्षामा प्रत्यक्ष प्रभाव पर्न सक्ने चिन्ता व्यक्त गरिन्छ ।

खासमा प्रधानमन्त्री शाहले राअविलाई बलियो बनाउने भनेरै जेठ १ गते कार्यविभाजन नियमावली संशोधन गर्दै प्रधानमन्त्री तथा मन्त्रिपरिषद्को कार्यालय मातहत लगेका थिए । तर साउन १० मा भएको सुनसरी घटनामा राअविले न प्रधानमन्त्रीको विश्वास जित्न सक्यो, न त प्रभावकारी सूचना नै दिन सक्यो ।

अहिले त राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान विभागलाई छाडेर नयाँ संरचना बनाउन पर्ने समेत आवज उठ्न थालेको छ ।

यस्तो छ गुप्तचर निकायको इतिहास ?

केन्द्रीय गुप्तचर विभागका रूपमा मंसिर २००८ मा स्थापना भएको राअवि विभिन्न समयमा नाम फेरिँदै अहिलेको अवस्थामा आइपुगेको हो । राअविकै सूचनाका आधारमा २०३२ साउन २७ गते नेपालस्थित एक दूतावासका अधिकारी मन्त्रिपरिषद्को माइन्युटसहित पक्राउ परेका थिए ।

यसमा तत्कालीन विद्युत् सहायकमन्त्री ध्यानबहादुर राईका निजी सचिव विजय चापागाईंसमेत मुछिएका थिए । २०५२ पछि माओवादी सशस्त्र संघर्ष उत्कर्षमा पुगेका बेला बेलायती खुफिया एजेन्सी एमआई–६ को सहयोगमा राअविले अपरेसन मुस्ताङ चलाएको थियो । कुनै बेला यो विभागलाई बाह्य जासुसी गर्ने जिम्मेवारीसमेत दिइएको थियो ।तर, २०४६ को परिवर्तनपछि यसलाई आन्तरिक गुप्तचरीको काममा मात्र सीमित गरियो ।

२०५० पछि यसलाई राजनीतिक दलले कार्यकर्ता भर्ती केन्द्र नै बनाएको देखिन्छ । संरचनागत रूपमा अहिले पनि राअवि पछाडि नै परेको देखिन्छ । यो विभागलाई नेपाली सेना, नेपाल प्रहरी र सशस्त्र प्रहरी बलपछि चौथो स्थानमा राखिएको छ। तर यो निकाय संवेदनशीलता र रणनीतिक महत्वका हिसाबले भने अग्रस्थानमा हुनुपर्ने हो । तर स्पष्ट संरचना र स्थायित्वको अभावका कारण यसको कार्यसम्पादन प्रभावित हुँदै आएको छ।

राअविको भूमिकामा राजनीतिक हस्तक्षेप बढ्दै जाँदा संस्था अझ कमजोर बन्दै गएको विश्लेषण भइरहेको छ। प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालय र गृह मन्त्रालयबीचको संरचनात्मक अस्पष्टताले पनि यसको कार्यक्षमतामा असर परेको देखिन्छ ।

articles.title: दैलेखको ग्यास परियोजना किन अलपत्र ?
articles.summary:
दैलेख । देशभर अहिले खाना पकाउने एलपी ग्यासको आपूर्ति सहज छैन । कतै उपभोक्ता सिलिन्डर बोकेर डिलरको ढोकामा लाइनमा छन्, कतै ग्यास पाउन दिनहुँ कुर्नुपर्ने अवस्था छ । ग्यास अभाव देखिँदा सर्वसाधारणको दैनिकी प्रभावित बनेको छ ।

एकातिर ग्यासको अभाव र आपूर्तिको चिन्ता छ, अर्कोतिर आफ्नै भूमिमा प्राकृतिक ग्यासको सम्भावना देखिएको परियोजना भने अहिले अलपत्र अवस्थामा छ ।

नेपालले हरेक वर्ष पेट्रोलियम पदार्थ र एलपी ग्यास आयातमा अर्बौं रुपैयाँ खर्च गर्दै आएको छ । अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा मूल्य वृद्धि वा आपूर्ति प्रभावित हुँदा त्यसको प्रत्यक्ष असर नेपाली उपभोक्ताले भोग्नुपर्छ । यता दैलेखको जलजले क्षेत्रमा प्राकृतिक ग्यासको सम्भावना देखिएको पेट्रोलियम अन्वेषण परियोजना भने पहिलो चरणको अध्ययनपछि अघि बढ्न सकेको छैन ।

नेपाल र चीन सरकारको सहकार्यमा सञ्चालित परियोजनाका लागि चीन सरकारले करिब २ अर्ब ४० करोड रुपैयाँ अनुदान दिएको थियो। चाइना जियोलोजिकल सर्भेले ४ हजार १३ मिटर गहिराइसम्म ड्रिलिङ गरी भूगर्भीय, भूभौतिक तथा भू–रासायनिक अध्ययन सम्पन्न गरेको थियो ।

अध्ययनले विशेषगरी मिथेन ग्यासको सम्भावना देखाएको छ । प्रतिवेदनले थप वेल टेस्टिङ गरी व्यावसायिक उत्पादनको सम्भाव्यता मूल्यांकन गर्न सिफारिस गरे पनि दोस्रो चरणको परीक्षण र लगानी योजना अघि बढ्न सकेको छैन । परियोजनाबाट रोजगारी र समृद्धिको आशामा स्थानीयले जग्गासमेत उपलब्ध गराएका थिए। तर योजना अलपत्र पर्ने हो कि भन्ने चिन्ता बढेको छ ।

रोजगारी र विकासको आशामा जग्गा दिएको स्थानीय बताउँछन् । तर यो परियोजना कागजमै सीमित हुने हो कि भन्ने चिन्ता उनीहरुमा देखिन्छ ।

देशको ऊर्जा भविष्यसँग जोडिएको यो परियोजनालाई स्थानीय, प्रदेश र संघीय सरकारले प्राथमिकताका साथ अघि बढाउनुपर्छ ।

दैलेखमा देखिएको सम्भावना प्रमाणित भई उत्पादन सुरु भए नेपाल ऊर्जा क्षेत्रमा आत्मनिर्भर बन्ने आधार तयार हुन सक्ने भैरवी गाउँपालिकाका अध्यक्षको भनाइ छ ।

यो परियोजनामा पहिलो चरणमा प्रयोग भएका उपकरण लामो समयदेखि प्रयोगविहीन छन् । तिनको संरक्षण र आगामी योजनाबारे स्पष्ट जानकारी सार्वजनिक भएको छैन ।

परियोजनालाई अघि बढाउने विषय सम्बन्धित निकायको निर्णय र समन्वयमा निर्भर छ । अहिले नेपाल ग्यास र पेट्रोलियम आयातमै निर्भर छ । दैलेखको जलजले परियोजनालाई समयमै अघि बढाउन सके दीर्घकालमा ऊर्जा आयात घटाउने महत्वपूर्ण आधार बन्न सक्ने देखिन्छ ।

articles.title: पढ्दै गर्दा नै विश्वव्यापी कम्पनीसँग काम गर्दै इस्लिङ्टन कलेजका २९ विद्यार्थी
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपालमै बसेर अध्ययनसँगै विश्वका विभिन्न कम्पनीका वास्तविक परियोजनामा काम गर्ने अवसर इस्लिङ्टन कलेजका २९ विद्यार्थीले पाएका छन् । कलेजले अघि सारेको ‘नेपालबाटै विश्वमा पहुँच’ भन्ने अवधारणालाई व्यवहारमै उतार्दै विद्यार्थीहरू अमेरिका, अस्ट्रेलिया र बेलायतका कम्पनीसँग जोडिएर अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय स्तरका परियोजनामा काम गरिरहेका हुन् ।

इस्लिङ्टन कलेजका लागि ‘नेपालबाटै विश्वमा पहुँच’ केवल प्रचारात्मक नारा नभई विद्यार्थीलाई देश नछोडीकनै विश्वस्तरमा प्रतिस्पर्धा गर्न सक्षम बनाउने शैक्षिक दृष्टिकोणका रूपमा अघि बढाइएको कलेजले जनाएको छ । यही उद्देश्यअनुसार कलेजले विभिन्न उद्योग तथा व्यावसायिक संस्थासँग सहकार्य गर्दै विद्यार्थीलाई पढाइसँगै व्यावहारिक अनुभव र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कार्य वातावरणमा काम गर्ने अवसर उपलब्ध गराउँदै आएको छ । कलेजका अनुसार विद्यार्थीले अध्ययनकै क्रममा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय स्तरको तालिम लिनुका साथै वास्तविक परियोजनामा सहभागी हुने अवसर पाउँछन् । यसका लागि डिग्री पूरा गर्नुपर्ने वा विदेश जानुपर्ने अवस्था छैन । काठमाडौंमै बसेर आफ्नो पढाइलाई निरन्तरता दिँदै उनीहरूले विश्वव्यापी टोलीसँग वास्तविक जिम्मेवारी सम्हालिरहेका छन् ।

अमेरिका, अस्ट्रेलिया र बेलायतका कम्पनीका लागि काम गरिरहेका २९ विद्यार्थीलाई कलेजले आफ्नो पहिलो कृत्रिम बौद्धिकता आधारित दक्ष विद्यार्थी समूहका रूपमा अघि सारेको छ । यी विद्यार्थीले आफ्नो मूल विषयसँगै आधुनिक कृत्रिम बौद्धिकता प्रविधिमा आधारित विश्वव्यापी कार्य वातावरणमा सोच्ने, निर्माण गर्ने र परिणाम दिन सक्ने सीप विकास गरेका छन् ।

कलेजले विद्यार्थीलाई वास्तविक परियोजना, उद्योगअनुकूल प्रयोगशाला, आधुनिक सुविधा र व्यावहारिक सिकाइमार्फत सुरुदेखि नै व्यावसायिक क्षेत्रका आवश्यकताअनुसार तयार पार्दै आएको जनाएको छ । त्यसकै परिणामस्वरूप विद्यार्थीहरू पढाइ पूरा हुनुअघि नै अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कम्पनीका वास्तविक काममा संलग्न हुन सफल भएको कलेजको दाबी छ ।

कलेजका अध्यक्ष सुलभ बुढाथोकीले विद्यार्थीले डिग्री पूरा गर्ने कि करियर सुरु गर्ने भन्ने दुईमध्ये एउटा रोज्नुपर्ने अवस्था नरहेको बताएका छन् । उनका अनुसार विद्यार्थीले अध्ययन र व्यावसायिक यात्रालाई एकसाथ अघि बढाइरहेका छन् ।

उनका अनुसार ‘नेपालबाटै विश्वमा पहुँच’ विद्यार्थीका लागि अवसर नेपालमै रहेको सन्देश दिने अभियानका रूपमा अघि बढाइएको हो । विद्यार्थीले अध्ययन पूरा गरेपछि मात्र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय क्षेत्रमा आफ्नो व्यावसायिक यात्रा सुरु गर्नुपर्ने सोच परिवर्तन हुँदै गएको उनको भनाइ छ । इस्लिङ्टन कलेजका विद्यार्थीलाई अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय परियोजनामा जोड्न विश्वव्यापी प्रविधि समूहसँग पनि सहकार्य गरिएको छ । यही सहकार्यअन्तर्गत २९ विद्यार्थी अमेरिका, अस्ट्रेलिया र बेलायतमा सञ्चालन भइरहेका विभिन्न परियोजनामा संलग्न छन् ।

यसैगरी, कृत्रिम बौद्धिकतामा आधारित बाह्य सेवा साझेदार संस्थाले पनि विद्यार्थीहरूको क्षमता र तयारीलाई सकारात्मक रूपमा मूल्यांकन गरेको छ । विश्वभरका प्रतिभाको खोजी, तालिम तथा प्रमाणीकरण गर्दै उनीहरूलाई व्यावसायिक टोलीसँग जोड्दै आएको उक्त संस्थाले सूचना प्रविधि विकास, डिजाइन, बजार व्यवस्थापन तथा सञ्चालनलगायतका क्षेत्रमा सहयोग गर्दै आएको बताइएको छ ।

उक्त संस्थाका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत प्रशान्त केसीका अनुसार इस्लिङ्टन कलेजका विद्यार्थी प्राविधिक रूपमा दक्ष छन् । नयाँ कुरा सिक्न सहज हुनुका साथै उनीहरू सुरुदेखि नै कृत्रिम बौद्धिकतामा आधारित कार्य वातावरणमा काम गर्न तयार देखिएको उनको भनाइ छ । कलेजले विद्यार्थीहरूको यो उपलब्धिलाई केवल अभ्यासका लागि गरिएको परियोजनाका रूपमा नभई वास्तविक व्यावसायिक अनुभवका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरेको छ । विद्यार्थीहरूले काठमाडौंमै बसेर आफ्नो नियमित अध्ययनलाई निरन्तरता दिँदै अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय टोलीमा जिम्मेवारी सम्हालिरहेका छन् । इस्लिङ्टन कलेजका अनुसार यसले नेपालमा अध्ययनरत विद्यार्थीका लागि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय अवसर प्राप्त गर्न विदेश नै जानुपर्ने वा अध्ययन पूरा भएपछि मात्र व्यावसायिक यात्रा सुरु गर्नुपर्ने परम्परागत सोचलाई समेत चुनौती दिएको छ । सही तालिम, प्रविधि, वातावरण र अवसर उपलब्ध गराउन सके नेपाली विद्यार्थीले नेपालमै बसेर विश्व बजारमा प्रतिस्पर्धा गर्न सक्ने कलेजको विश्वास छ ।

कलेजको पहिलो कृत्रिम बौद्धिकता आधारित दक्ष विद्यार्थी समूहले पनि यही सम्भावनालाई व्यवहारमा प्रमाणित गरेको दाबी गरिएको छ । विद्यार्थीका लागि विश्वसँग काम गर्ने अवसर स्नातकपछि मात्र सुरु हुने नभई पढाइसँगै सुरु हुन सक्ने उदाहरणका रूपमा यसलाई लिइएको छ ।

यससँगै ‘नेपालबाटै विश्वमा पहुँच’ अब इस्लिङ्टन कलेजको अभियान वा नारामा मात्र सीमित नभई विद्यार्थीले नेपालमै बसेर अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कम्पनीसँग काम गर्दै हासिल गरिरहेको वास्तविक अनुभव र उपलब्धिका रूपमा स्थापित हुँदै गएको कलेजले जनाएको छ ।

articles.title: Nepali Students can now transfer academic credits between universities
articles.summary:
Students who have had to discontinue their studies or move to another university will now be able to transfer the academic credits they have earned and continue their education under a new system introduced by the University Grants Commission (UGC).

The UGC has issued the Academic Credit Bank Establishment and Operation Directive 2026, setting common standards for storing and transferring credits earned at universities and other higher education institutions in Nepal and abroad. The directive, made public on Friday, aims to make credit transfer more transparent and consistent among universities.

“Universities can carry out credit transfers. The directive has been issued to establish a credit bank, but much work remains before the bank can be fully operational,” said Kedar Prasad Acharya, director at the UGC. “It will take some time.”

The commission plans to establish the Academic Credit Bank itself. Under the directive, credits earned by students will be stored on a single digital platform and can later be transferred, at their request, to another institution or another programme within the same institution.

Nepali universities have been allowing credit transfers through their own arrangements, but there has been no common standard or formal system recognised across institutions. The UGC decided in April to introduce a national framework for credit transfer and subsequently prepared the directive.

Former UGC chair Devaraj Adhikari said the absence of clear and uniform rules had made credit transfers difficult in Nepal. “Standards have been set to make credit transfer easier by bringing uniformity,” he said. “Universities can work according to the directive.”

Adhikari said the system would particularly benefit students who return to Nepal after having to stop their studies abroad, those who need to change universities for various reasons and people who leave or resume higher education while working.

The need for a common system gained attention after the death of a Nepali student at Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology in Odisha, India, in February 2025. Following the incident, Nepali students studying there announced plans to discontinue their studies. Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu University and Purbanchal University subsequently offered to admit affected students through credit transfer, but each institution followed different criteria.

Acharya said the new directive was intended to remove such inconsistencies. “The directive provides a uniform basis for credit transfer, which universities can implement through their own academic rules,” he said.

The proposed Academic Credit Bank will serve as a digital, virtual and online repository of academic credits earned at higher education institutions. Students will have to apply to deposit their credits in the system. The credits can then be transferred after the receiving institution determines that the subjects and academic fields are sufficiently equivalent.

The system will also apply to students who studied at institutions established under the laws of foreign countries, including those who interrupted their studies midway.

However, there are limits. Credits earned for a bachelor’s degree can be transferred and used only within seven years, while those for a master’s degree can be transferred within five years. The amount transferred cannot exceed 50 percent of the total credits required for the programme in which a student seeks admission.

Universities will also have to record transferred credits on the academic certificate issued to students. The UGC said the directive was designed to promote student mobility and continuity in higher education by allowing credits earned inside and outside Nepal to be accumulated and transferred.

The directive allows federal and provincial universities, as well as academies, to amend their rules and regulations to implement the provisions. Universities have generally treated 16 hours of learning under the semester system as equivalent to one academic credit.

Officials say the new framework could be especially useful for students whose education is disrupted by unforeseen circumstances. Rather than forcing them to start a degree again after changing institutions, the system will allow them to carry forward eligible academic work.

The commission says the digital credit bank will eventually provide a national record of students’ academic credits, although its full operation will require further technical and administrative work.

articles.title: Insurance scheme to benefit small businesses
articles.summary:
Nepal has brought into force an insurance scheme aimed at protecting small businesses from risks that can disrupt their operations and income.

The first-of-its-kind policy, targeting small retail and service businesses such as fruit shops, motorcycle workshops, tailoring businesses and plumbing services, came into effect with the start of the new fiscal year in mid-July.

For instance, if a fruit shop owner is injured or hospitalised, the policy will cover lost income if the shop has to close.

Nirmal Adhikari, director of the Nepal Insurance Authority, said insurance penetration among Nepal’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) remains severely low and that the new policy is the first step towards addressing the vulnerabilities of the sector.

He said microinsurance has largely been implemented through cooperatives and community business groups but has failed to reach MSMEs as expected.

“It’s because of limited awareness, weak distribution channels and inadequate public understanding of insurance,” Adhikari said.

Last week, a joint report by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Nepal and the Nepal Insurance Authority was launched, finding that MSMEs, particularly those operating in agriculture and tourism, remain dangerously underinsured.

Existing insurance products fail to cover many of the risks faced by these businesses, leaving them highly vulnerable to climate shocks, disease, pandemics and income losses, according to the report, titled Risk Management in Nepal's MSMEs: The Insurance Protection Gap.

Formal insurance has failed to adequately address the diverse risks faced by MSMEs despite agriculture and tourism being among Nepal’s key economic sectors.

Only about 10 percent of MSMEs in Nepal currently hold any form of insurance. Small businesses face heavy exposure to climate-induced hazards, natural disasters and unexpected business disruptions.

Cumbersome paperwork and unclear policy terms mean existing payouts often cover only a fraction of actual losses.

Based on surveys and focus group discussions involving 134 MSME representatives across the seven provinces, the study found that agriculture-based MSMEs face acute climate, disease and credit-related risks that current insurance products do not adequately cover.

Tourism MSMEs, meanwhile, remain fragile after the Covid-19 pandemic and continue to face significant indirect risks with limited insurance protection.

According to the report, insurance products currently available do not reflect the actual needs of MSMEs, leading many entrepreneurs to view insurance as costly, inaccessible and irrelevant.

In agriculture, insurance products mainly cover crops and livestock while ignoring indirect risks such as income loss, credit defaults and supply chain disruptions, according to the report.

“Although weather index insurance was introduced as an innovative solution, poor calibration means rainfall and temperature triggers often fail to match actual field-level losses, leaving insured farmers without compensation,” the report said.

The report said slow claims processing, lengthy paperwork and unclear eligibility requirements further discourage smallholder farmers from purchasing insurance.

In tourism, insurance coverage is largely limited to vehicles and property, leaving major risks such as business interruption, liability for accidents or employee injuries, and pandemic-related disruptions largely uninsured.

Claims processing, even for mandatory vehicle insurance, is often delayed and disputed, reducing confidence in insurance providers.

Weak distribution networks in rural and peri-urban areas, coupled with high transaction costs, have also limited insurers’ outreach to smaller businesses.

The report further said misconceptions about insurance continue to undermine public trust.

“Many agriculture entrepreneurs mistakenly believe insurance only applies to catastrophic events or expect guaranteed financial returns similar to savings schemes. When claims are rejected or payouts do not reflect actual losses, these misconceptions are reinforced,” according to the report.

“Similarly, many tourism entrepreneurs believe insurance is meant only for large businesses.”

The report attributes these perceptions to low insurance literacy and inadequate communication by insurers.

Despite these challenges, the report says the sectors present significant opportunities for insurers.

In agriculture, provinces such as Karnali, Koshi and Madhesh, where vulnerabilities are high but insurance uptake remains low, offer commercially viable markets if products are redesigned to suit local conditions and distributed through trusted community networks.

The report recommends bundled insurance products that combine protection against climate, livestock, business continuity and credit risks to better meet MSMEs’ needs while improving insurers’ commercial viability.

For the tourism sector, it suggests simplified claims procedures and products covering business continuity and liability risks.

Bundling insurance with licensing, accreditation or association membership could also expand coverage, particularly among trekking, hospitality and seasonal tourism businesses.

Adhikari said the Nepal Insurance Authority has directed insurance companies to market the new product through organised groups to improve outreach.

Nepal has more than 923,000 businesses, over 95 percent of them microenterprises.

These businesses contributed an estimated 22 to 27 percent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) and accounted for more than 84 percent of non-agricultural employment.

The report says a handful of SME-focused insurance products exist, but most are narrowly targeted.

For example, the Youth and SME Insurance Policy is available only to borrowers under the Youth and Small Entrepreneur Self-Development Fund.

Although the government has prioritised expanding insurance coverage through the 16th Five-Year Plan (2024-25 to 2028-29) and introduced the Microinsurance Directive, 2023, requiring insurers to allocate 10 percent of their portfolios to microinsurance implementation has been slow.

Insurers cite a lack of incentives, skilled personnel and technological infrastructure as major obstacles to expanding non-life insurance coverage.

The report said the shortage of innovative and inclusive insurance products forces many MSMEs either to purchase multiple policies that cover only a fraction of their risks or rely on informal coping mechanisms such as personal savings, family support, small loans, cost-cutting measures and business diversification.

According to the report, while access to credit has received considerable policy attention, financial risk management through insurance remains largely neglected, leaving most MSMEs exposed to financial shocks and undermining their long-term growth prospects.

articles.title: Past outbreaks offer little lesson as Japanese encephalitis deaths rise
articles.summary:
At least nine people have died and 37 others have been infected with Japanese encephalitis (JE) virus in less than a month, and health officials warn that the toll could rise as the peak season for the mosquito-borne disease approaches.

What has particularly concerned immunisation officials is the death of a person in Nawalparasi East, where authorities had launched a JE vaccination campaign a few months ago.

“Our surveillance and investigation show that the person who died of JE infection was unvaccinated,” said Dr Abhiyan Gautam, chief of Immunisation Section at the Family Welfare Division under the Department of Health Services. “Coverage of JE vaccination in Nawalparasi East was only 77 percent and the recent death shows that unvaccinated people are at risk of getting seriously ill or dying from the infection.”

JE is a viral brain infection endemic to Asia and parts of the Western Pacific. It is transmitted by mosquitoes and belongs to the same flavivirus family as dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and West Nile viruses.

The virus kills about one-third of those who develop severe illness, while up to half of survivors are left with severe lifelong disabilities, according to the World Health Organisation.

Six of the nine deaths were reported in Koshi province, two in Madhesh and one in Lumbini. Health authorities are probing other reported deaths and infections.

Last year, 41 people died and 141 others were infected with JE, which spread to over 117 local units across 45 districts. The case fatality rate was around 23 percent.

In 2024, 23 people, including one person in Kathmandu Valley, died of JE, while at least 80 were infected.

Around 20 percent of the cases reported this year have resulted in deaths. Officials say unvaccinated people are at serious risk of getting severe and dying from the infection. The disease can cause permanent injuries to the brain and the nervous system, and there is no specific treatment. Care focuses on managing symptoms and complications.

Immunisation experts and members of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee have recommended a single dose of the JE vaccine for all unvaccinated people, saying they remain at high risk of infection, severe illness, and death.

Last year’s data show that 76 percent of those who died from JE were over 40 years old, while around 70 percent of those infected were older than 15. The figures indicate that the disease is affecting a large number of people beyond the age group coerced by routine childhood vaccination.

Asked why authorities have not taken broader preventive measures after 41 people died of JE last year, officials say vaccination was the only effective measure to prevent infection and deaths, but the government did not have the budget to vaccinate all vulnerable populations.

“We know that vaccination is a safe and proven method to prevent deaths, permanent disabilities and infection from JE,” said Gautam. “We know that we can save our population by a single dose of vaccine.

But the government did not have the budget to vaccinate the entire population at once, he said. “We only managed to launch vaccination in Nawalparasi East and some wards of Chitwan districts, where the infection rate was too high.”

The government has allocated Rs460 million to vaccinate people in 11 districts with a high JE burden. Chitwan, Kailali, Tanahun, Dang, Jhapa, Kapilvastu, Morang, Rupandehi, Sunsari, Rautahat and Sarlahi districts have been selected for the campaign based on their high morbidity and mortality rates.

However, the vaccination programme will not start before April next year, because vaccine procurement and supply will take time, according to officials.

JE has long been a major public health problem in Nepal. The virus killed nearly 2,000 people in Nepal in 2005, mostly children in the Tarai districts.

Nepal started administering the JE vaccine in 2006, eight years before the WHO officially issued prequalification certification, due to high rates of infection and deaths. The programme was later expanded with support from donors and global health partners.

Experts say everyone who remains unvaccinated should receive at least one dose of the JE vaccine, which is effective in preventing severe illness and death.

“As JE infection causes high mortality and disability, authorities concerned must arrange the vaccine for the unvaccinated population,” said Dr Shyam Raj Upreti, former director general at the Department of Health Services.

Upreti, who is also an immunisation expert, said vaccination is the only effective way to prevent further deaths and disabilities from JE.

Along with vaccination, awareness drives and promotion of sanitation and hygiene and behavioural change are also crucial in preventing the spread of the deadly viral disease.

Officials say the responsibility for public awareness drives lies with the local governments. However, poor coordination among the three tiers of government — federal, provincial and local — has hampered other preventive measures. Many local governments say they do not even receive timely information about JE outbreaks.

Nepal has included the JE vaccine in its routine immunisation programme and administers it free of charge to children at state-run health facilities.

An estimated 12.5 million people are thought to be at high risk of JE infection in Nepal.

The vaccine is also available at pharmacies, but it is costly, meaning that many vulnerable people cannot afford to pay out of pocket.

JE is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes. Pigs and ducks are considered natural reservoirs of the virus. Pig farmers and those residing near the paddy fields are at particularly high risk.

articles.title: Q&A: You can distract the public with talk of intentions for a while, but it isn’t sustainable
articles.summary:
As Nepal approaches the first anniversary of the historic Gen Z protests, the political landscape remains fraught with tension, high expectations and mounting frustration. Born from the momentum of a movement that demanded sweeping reform, good governance and accountability, the current administration under Prime Minister Balendra Shah finds itself under intense scrutiny.

The Post’s Biken K Dawadi sat down with prominent social activist from the Gen Z age group, Rakshya Bam, in her first interview since the March elections, to discuss the state of the nation, dissecting the government’s response to recent communal clashes in Tarai-Madhesh, the systemic shortcomings in police riot control, and a perceived absence of empathy in urban governance. From concerns over digital authoritarianism and shrinking spaces for civic dissent to deep-seated structural neglect in marginalised regions like Sudurpashchim, the discussion cuts to the heart of contemporary Nepali politics. As critics weigh the rhetoric of ‘clean intentions’ against administrative reality, the conversation explores whether the state is genuinely fulfilling the democratic mandate carved out by its citizens or if, as some fear, this government is veering dangerously off course.

To begin with current affairs, how do you evaluate the government’s response to the communal clashes in Madhesh, which critics have described as both inadequate and delayed?

In regard to the incidents in Madhesh, we were all waiting for an address from the Prime Minister. Once that address finally came, it did provide a sense of relief, even for those of us sitting here in the capital. Hearing the news that Prime Minister Balendra Shah, as the guardian of the nation, was finally addressing the situation was something we were anticipating. However, while we felt that relief, my thoughts immediately went to those living in the heart of the clashes and the riots. I couldn’t help but wonder what they were experiencing and feeling in that moment. I firmly believe that a state’s primary priority must always be its citizens. Had the PM addressed the Sunsari incident on the first or second day, perhaps fewer bullets would have been fired, and fewer lives would have been lost. Whether an address comes five days or ten days later, it is still an address, but the priority should have been on minimising damage and resolving the crisis effectively.

Do you believe the government, which came to power with a significant mandate following the Gen Z protests, truly required five days to formulate a ‘national security strategy’ before the Home Minister visited the field?

What occurred in Sunsari was more than just an isolated problem. It was a full-blown crisis. In such situations, you don’t just solve the issue; you have to deal with it through immediate engagement. There was a desperate need for representatives to be on the ground, speaking with every community. If the presence of the Prime Minister or the Home Minister on the field could save even a single life, then why wouldn’t they go immediately? The Home Minister did eventually go, but only after five days. He mentioned in interviews with The Post and Kantipur that they were in Kathmandu for those five days developing a ‘national strategy’. But what exactly is this ‘national strategy’? He didn’t elaborate. If a strategy to simply go and talk to these groups takes five days to create, then I find that hard to believe. Such things should be clear within a single day. While we are relieved the riots stopped, there are many areas where the government’s approach needs great improvement for the future.

Given that the police response in Madhesh appeared to involve indiscriminate and disproportionate force, similar to what was seen during the Gen Z protests of September, do you feel the state has failed to learn any lessons regarding the protection of general lives?

I see this as a systemic failure rather than just the fault of individual officers. When we look back at the Gen Z movement, we saw the position the police were put in and the resulting distance and atmosphere of fear that developed between the youth and the security forces. I blame the system and those leading the institutions for this because the system isn’t providing the police with the necessary resources or clear criteria for riot control. In the Sunsari riots, all the public knows is that bullets were fired. We don’t know the actual process or criteria the police were supposed to follow. The state needs to invest in the police and ensure they understand their primary role is to save lives, not take them. There is a massive difference between a trained professional using a weapon and an untrained person. The state must invest in proper training and equipment.

Regarding the portrayal of these clashes as inter-religious conflict, what steps do you believe are necessary to foster genuine communal harmony in the Tarai-Madhesh region?

While we should wait for the official reports before reaching definitive conclusions about who was behind the unrest, it is clear from the outside that religious tensions, particularly between Hindu and Muslim communities, are being stirred. Our society has a long history of living together in harmony. There is a saying that when you sleep on the same pillow, you might occasionally kick each other, and perhaps that is what is happening now. But we must never forget the essence: We are all human beings. No religion teaches us to hate one another. In fact, the more diverse the religions, the more there is to learn from one another. I am reminded of something Javed Akhtar once quoted: “If I am only ‘I’, then what is ‘I’? If you are only ‘you’, then what is ‘you’?” This is the core philosophy of secularism—respecting all religions. It is not about insulting others or imposing your beliefs, but about finding a balance between ‘yourness’ and ‘my-ness’.

Let’s change track. How do you interpret the way in which some Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) MPs have started speaking out quite strongly against the very government they are part of?

This is a standard parliamentary process. An MP has every right to voice their concerns to the Prime Minister, the House, or the Speaker. We are often accused of wanting to topple this government or wishing for its failure, but that is completely untrue. If this government fails, we—those of us who campaigned for change—will be the ones who face the most criticism. This government was formed on the momentum of our movement, with a mandate for change, good governance and reform. For the sake of public sentiment and the votes cast, this government must succeed. Our questions are not meant to harm the government. They are meant to make it successful, accountable and responsible. I believe the PM needs to be more wary of the people immediately surrounding him—his ‘team’—rather than our questions. The fact that even his own party’s MPs are protesting suggests there is a problem with his pattern of working.

When the PM claims he has ‘good intentions’ but admits he may not always follow the established processes, how do you evaluate such a narrative?

The narrative of ‘good intentions’ is something we hear a lot, even in his social media updates, but having clean intentions is not enough on its own. This must be demonstrated through actions. We have to ask: What are your intentions regarding the Constitution? What are your intentions regarding your attendance in the House? What about your intentions toward state institutions, the police, inclusivity and democracy itself? You cannot claim clean intentions while disregarding the process. What the public ultimately needs is a functioning system. If we don’t build a system now, what happens if the next PM doesn’t have ‘clean intentions’? You can distract the public with talk of intentions for a while, but it isn’t sustainable. We need results.

Is it appropriate for a PM to communicate vital national updates and responses to parliamentary questions primarily through Facebook posts?

It isn’t appropriate at all. We don’t always know what the Prime Minister is doing because the PMO’s information flow to the citizens is often ineffective. We have to ask if the information being provided is accessible to everyone. For instance, how does the government communicate with citizens who are visually impaired or those who are deaf? To truly connect with the people, there needs to be direct engagement, perhaps a weekly address where the public is informed about the government’s work. The PM holds the highest political power; he should be making the public feel his presence as a guardian. Remaining silent and only posting on social media is not a healthy sign for a democracy.

Since transparency was a foundation of the Gen Z movement, do you believe the first elected government following those protests is failing to meet those standards?

I wouldn’t say there is no transparency at all, but there is a disconnect in how it is practised. Transparency should be about empowering the citizens. The main question is: Who is the government facing? For example, a local government might post its reports on a website and claim transparency. But if those reports are filled with such dense legal jargon that an ordinary citizen cannot understand them, then how is that truly transparent? It’s more like ‘semi-transparency’. While we can’t say transparency is entirely absent just because the PM doesn’t address the public directly, in a democracy, direct dialogue with the people is essential.

As a prominent face of dissent outside of Parliament, how do you respond to the increasingly aggressive and negative reactions you face in digital spaces?

There is a concerted effort to shrink the space for dissent, but we shouldn’t allow it to happen. When we used to pose questions to previous governments, the response was never this irrational or irrelevant. Now, there is so much negativity, and chaos is spread to attack anyone who speaks up. However, it doesn’t matter to me if someone sitting in a room in Lalitpur writes a negative comment about me. What matters is my conviction. For younger activists, I would say you must anticipate that the path will be difficult. In Nepal today, activists are often viewed through a negative lens, despite the good work they have achieved. You must hold onto your convictions and, if faced with digital harassment, remember there are legal avenues like the Cyber Bureau.

Given the government’s handling of squatter settlements and the use of force without prior management, do you feel there is a fundamental lack of empathy in their governance?

There is zero empathy and no compassion. The way bulldozers were used in squatter settlements was unjustifiable, not just for today but for the future of Nepal’s history. Perhaps it would be different if the PM admitted it was a mistake, but displacing people without any prior management plan is a violation of their constitutional rights. This goes back to the ‘clean intentions’ issue—the PM might say his intentions are clean, but if he ignores the constitutional right of every citizen to live with dignity, then his intentions are irrelevant. Watching children, pregnant women, and the elderly crying while the settlements were destroyed was a spectacle of indignity. The government failed to maintain the dignity of its citizens and ignored the proper process.

How do you respond to the common argument that the public should ‘let the government work’ before offering criticism, considering this government is still in its early months?

It surprises me when people say ‘let them work’. Have we tied up the government’s hands? Is the government so fragile that our words prevent them from doing their jobs? We aren’t stopping them; we are asking for accountability. We are saying they are responsible for their actions and must provide answers. Questioning should be allowed from Day One. There is a massive amount of hope placed in this government, and both the public and the government are afraid that this hope will turn into disappointment. We don’t want that to happen, but currently, it feels like the government is on the wrong track. We ask questions precisely to keep them on the right path.

In light of the Gen Z movement’s stance against nepotism, how do you view the government’s current appointments and its approach to meritocracy?

The government claims the people they surround themselves with are the most capable, and we are expected to believe that. However, in a country as diverse as ours, meritocracy alone isn’t enough. We have marginalised communities and regions where people have significantly less access to power. Representation must reflect our geography and our diverse communities. The state isn’t a private company. It’s a public institution funded by taxpayers like us. In exchange for my taxes, I expect basic services. For example, in the entire Sudurpashchim province, there isn’t a single nephrologist. If we need our kidneys checked, we have to wait for a camp or a visiting doctor once a month. People are losing their lives because they can’t get an ICU bed in a district hospital. When I see the lack of representation for Sudurpashchim in state institutions, I feel like we should just amend the Constitution to officially label Sudurpashchim as ‘Second-Class Nepal’. At least then we wouldn’t have any expectations. It’s heartbreaking to see how much the state can neglect a region in terms of health, education and basic infrastructure.

As we approach the first anniversary of the Gen Z protests, how would you evaluate the progress made compared to your expectations when you first took to the streets?

The political cycle of a country moves in its own way. When I went to the streets on September 8 and 9, I couldn’t have imagined the situation that would follow. We went with the simple hope for a bright future for the country. Since then, an interim government held elections, and the Constitution and democracy are back on track with an elected PM. That is a reason to be happy. While the government has made numerous mistakes, I think it is still a bit too early to judge them completely. We want corruption to be eradicated, but that won’t happen overnight. We want good governance, though the definition of that varies—for some, it’s better roads and no traffic; for others, it’s the rule of law. Our society is currently in a state of disorder, and we must head towards good governance. I hope this government moves in that direction, but we must be very careful right now.

If you had to give a rating or a sense of where we are currently in terms of the government’s performance, what would it be?

It’s difficult to say if things have improved or declined because the government has given us so many headaches over the last four months. We can’t openly say they are doing a great job, yet side-by-side, the country is functioning. Administrative work is happening, and the government is managing the country’s responsibilities, which is significant in itself. However, where the government is failing is in its actual presence for the people—like providing healthcare where there is none.

So, in Gen Z terminology, is it a ‘6-7’?

Yes. In conclusion, I’d say we are at ‘6-7’.

articles.title: Strengthen public service platforms amid rising public frustration
articles.summary:
Delivering seamless digital governance was one of the Rastriya Swatantra Party’s ambitious election agendas. After winning the election and assuming office in March, it set out a 100-point good governance plan that promised reforms in taxes, healthcare, agriculture and accountability to enable seamless public service delivery. Initially, it upgraded the Hello Sarkar grievance platform to operate 24 hours a day. It introduced paperless processing for passports, citizenship certificates and driving licences through the Nagarik App and cleared the backlog of smart driving licences. The emphasis on technology and digital governance in the reform agenda, along with the actions taken since assuming office in the sector, is commendable. Still, it is not doing enough to resolve the long-standing issues that hinder the country’s ambition for digital governance.

Frequent server crashes, operational bottlenecks and prolonged service outages are forcing people to navigate a complex bureaucratic maze and leave without completing essential administrative work. For instance, the Nepal Rastra Bank requires citizens to obtain a National Identity Card to open bank accounts. The government has a basic obligation to ensure that the platform to apply for it works. Yet the underlying database frequently collapses under peak traffic, creating bottlenecks nationwide. Other services that frequently go down include immigration services, passport issuance, land registration, transport management, licence renewals and tax payments.

The problem has long been ailing the public, but the urgency to tackle it is lacking. Successive governments have failed to make digital platforms work because of flawed planning and a weak system. Once installed, digital technologies require constant investment in maintenance, upgrades, patching and technical expertise and IT professionals, but governments haven’t put in the effort to keep them running, rendering them useless after a few years. Additionally, officials heavily rely on foreign technology firms for critical government systems. While there is nothing wrong with using that expertise, local workers often cannot resolve the problem independently when the system goes down. Procurement committees constantly buying cheap, short-lived systems that require long, bureaucratic delays to maintain is also creating a massive backlog for citizens. Concomitantly, with the focus on purchasing physical assets, software issues, such as their maintenance, are sidelined, leading to security vulnerabilities.

Given the widespread server crashes, it’s high time Nepal overhauls its digital systems. The government cannot continue to disregard maintenance to the point that the system completely breaks down and fails to serve the public. Any serious investment in a digital system must involve maintaining and upgrading it from the outset. The procurement process also warrants reform in line with rapidly changing technology. Moreover, rather than fully depending on foreign expertise, the government must utilise and retain the country’s young talent in the engineering and IT sector to manage critical government systems independently.

This government carries the immense trust of a public eager for reforms, which presents both a great opportunity and a responsibility to address the problems and take digital governance to a better level. It cannot afford to waste this chance.

articles.title: Nepal needs to rethink its antimicrobial resistance strategy
articles.summary:
Many people have heard about antibiotics, but do not precisely know what this medicine is and how it works, let alone what antimicrobial resistance (AMR) means. Yet, many have wondered why some infections become difficult to treat, even when antimicrobials are available. Do antimicrobials always work against infections? The fact remains that infectious agents, such as bacteria, do spontaneously develop resistance over time. But this process can be accelerated when bacteria are repeatedly exposed to antimicrobials, including through unnecessary or inappropriate use.

For the past several years, studies have consistently shown that Nepal, like other South Asian countries, experiences excessive and inappropriate use of antimicrobials. In urban areas, one can easily walk into a drug shop, explain symptoms and buy antibiotics, often without a prescription. A patient with a common cold may demand antibiotics even though antibiotics do not work against viruses.

But this is only one side of Nepal’s story. Travel to remote areas, and the problem may be the opposite. For populations in far-flung villages, access to even basic and essential antimicrobials can be difficult. A bacterial infection that could have been treated relatively easily could become severe and complicated. By the time the patient reaches a hospital, treatment can be more complicated and much more expensive.

This is the tension between access and excess. In one place, antimicrobials are easily available and consumed unnecessarily; in another, people who genuinely need them struggle to obtain them. Here lies the unsettling heterogeneity of who becomes vulnerable and who does not, and who needs attention and who, relatively, does not. This is the first premise where community engagement can offer solutions.

Such contradictions in Nepal’s supply side and demand side cannot simply be fixed by bombarding people with recommendations about ‘appropriate antibiotic use’. In such scenarios, stakeholder analysis allows one to explore a multitude of interests and their interactions, understand why people behave as they do, and analyse how health systems, pharmacies, patients, farmers and communities function within their own circumstances and in relation to each other. This is the second premise where community engagement can help resolve the puzzle.

Yet, engagement strategies have sometimes been given unequal weight, particularly with a preference for participatory and dialogue-based activities over approaches that prioritise breadth of engagement. In practice, however, both approaches can and need to coexist, often complementing each other.

Historically, experts developed recommendations at the centre, bureaucracies converted them into programmes, and instructions travelled downward through the health system until they eventually reached communities. Nepal is familiar with this model where a guideline is prepared in Kathmandu, training is provided at the provincial or district level, posters reach health facilities, and communities are told what behaviour should change. Inadequate community buy-in as such can undermine the entire effort.

The one-way nature of vertical engagement has also been rightly criticised. Experts and bureaucrats may prescribe solutions for communities whose everyday experiences are radically different from their own. Recommendations can be technically sound and well-intentioned but also poorly grounded and unrealistic. Imagine telling a person in a remote village that antibiotics must only be taken after consulting a qualified doctor when reaching that doctor requires a day’s walk and considerable expense. Or telling a small poultry farmer to simply reduce antimicrobial use without discussing veterinary access, disease prevention and the possibility that losing chickens may mean losing the household’s income.

Participatory engagement has enormous value. Community members can be involved from the outset, contribute to identifying problems, setting agendas, designing interventions, implementing activities, and evaluating results. Such involvement can garner trust, ownership and produce interventions grounded in local realities. Patients may explain why they avoid health facilities. Farmers may describe why antimicrobials are important for protecting their livestock. These conversations can reveal problems that an expert sitting in Kathmandu may never see.

But enthusiasm for deep participation should not lead us to undervalue another dimension of engagement—breadth. Nepal’s experience with vaccination, mass drug administration and public health campaigns demonstrates the value of reaching hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions, of people. Radio, television, schools, social media, health facilities and community networks can carry simple messages about antibiotics across enormous populations.

Such breadth-based engagement may lack the depth of a small participatory meeting, but its scale is precisely the strength. A community dialogue involving 30 people can uncover why antibiotics are misused in one municipality. A nationwide radio campaign can make hundreds of thousands think twice before demanding antibiotics for a viral cold. Why must one be considered inherently superior to the other?

This is precisely where diagonal community engagement becomes useful. It combines vertical, population-wide strategies with bottom-up, participatory and dialogue-based engagement. This is particularly relevant for Nepal as it is efficient for low- and middle-income countries. AMR is a super-wicked problem. It involves human health, animal health, agriculture, food systems, pharmacies, hospitals, sanitation, environmental contamination, regulation, economics and human behaviour. There will never be one community, one message or one intervention capable of addressing all these dimensions.

Nepal therefore needs engagement that can travel in both directions. Scientific evidence, surveillance, regulation and national communication must move outward from institutions to communities. At the same time, experiences, constraints and solutions emerging from communities must travel back towards policymakers and researchers. Health governance, in other words, should re-orient the approach to reap benefits from a combination of conventional vertical and more recent participatory approaches.

For AMR control, while relevant to many other public health interventions, the idea is to blend these approaches to reach millions at scale and listen deeply to socio-cultural features while identifying and safeguarding vulnerabilities.

articles.title: The case for Indigenous political thought
articles.summary:
“A child of the Earth goes back to the Earth.A child of the Sun goes back to the Sun.A child of the Moon goes back to the Moon.”

This sacred passage from the Mundhum is recited in dialogic form by Tutu-tumyahangs—learned elders and keepers of Indigenous wisdom—during Limbu Indigenous death ceremonies. At first glance, these lines speak of human mortality. Read more closely, however, they express a profound Indigenous political thought: Human existence is inseparable from the Earth and the wider cosmos, and life is sustained through relationships of reciprocity rather than domination. Embedded within this brief passage is a political philosophy that understands nature not as property to be possessed or exploited, but as the source of life to which all beings ultimately return.

As Nepal marks its 31st Indigenous Peoples’ Day, the government, policymakers and those engaged in the country’s development would do well to pay closer attention to the dozens of Indigenous communities whose diverse political traditions and philosophies have long sustained their societies. These Indigenous political thoughts are living intellectual traditions that offer vital insights for reimagining Nepal’s development, deepening its democracy, and building a more just peace as the country confronts profound political and environmental challenges.

It is useful to consider what political thought is, and how Indigenous political thought might help us reimagine our present and future by recognising the diversity of thinking and being.

In The Rights of War and Peace, historian Richard Tuck divides political thought into the ancient and the modern—the former being collectivistic and the latter individualistic. More broadly, he explains that such thought emerges and evolves in response to defining historical and contemporary political, economic and social crises. The emergence of the liberal order in the post-World War II period, its gradual demise, and the rise of China shaping the world order are examples of such dynamics. Another historian, Richard Whatmore, conceives of political thought—whether Western or ‘Oriental’—as full of complexities and paradoxes: sacred, tragic, nationalistic and utopian, shaped by time and space. Today, we witness such complexities: People are wealthier than in the 1900s, yet inequality is stark; societies are more technologically sophisticated, yet these advances have deepened—or will deepen—divisions; and while some countries are better able to withstand escalating climate harms, others face existential threats. At this crossroads, Indigenous political thought offers a space to reimagine the future.

To be sure, Indigenous political thought has not only always existed, but has also profoundly shaped global trade, world politics, economics and science for centuries. The idea of egalitarianism, interdependence and autonomy—some key tenets of liberalism—is said to be drawn from North American Indigenous thought.

In Asia, as James Scott states, most Indigenous communities maintained political autonomy and self-governance guided by their own philosophical traditions, away from modern states, including by resisting colonial subjugation up until the late 19th century. This is certainly the case for various Indigenous communities in Nepal and many other South and Southeast Asian countries that lived under their own governance structures. Like (non-Indigenous) political thought, Indigenous political thought also evolved in response to colonial contexts. At its core, the thought is not a set of abstract political theories centred on modern-state sovereignty and its sanctioned legal order; rather, it is grounded in the right to self-determination, governance based on reciprocity, legal pluralism, collectivity, forgiveness, reconciliation rooted in history, place (land), relationship and spirituality.

To understand Indigenous political thought, one need not be Indigenous. Nor is discussing it an attempt to dismiss or displace non-Indigenous political thought. Rather, it broadens the intellectual terrain of political inquiry and at times helps explore impossibilities.
