While the former has endured through centuries of colonial violence and continues to evolve, the latter has generated diverse, often competing traditions—some associated with empire, colonialism, fascism, Nazism, communism and capitalism; others with democracy, constitutionalism, human rights and emancipation. Political thought, be it Indigenous or non-Indigenous, has never been singular; it has always emerged from particular histories, places and struggles.

Unfortunately, academic discussion, including policymaking spaces, often approaches political thought through a reductive framework of right and wrong, celebrating some traditions while dismissing others. Such an approach forecloses dialogue and obscures the historical conditions from which political ideas and new policy interventions emerge. The task of engaging Indigenous political thought, therefore, is neither to talk back to the canon nor merely to look back at history. Rather, it is to move the conversation forward while remaining attentive to the legacies of historical violence, dispossession and injustice, as well as to moments of political innovation and transformation.

Addressing climate crises and advancing justice, forgiveness and reconciliation—at least from legal and humanistic perspectives—are grounded in principles long articulated within Indigenous political thought. In 2021, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres urged humanity to end its “senseless and suicidal war with nature.” Building on this call, the 2024 UN Biodiversity Conference (COP16) called humanity to live “in balance and in harmony with Mother Earth” while recognising the knowledge, innovations and practices of Indigenous Peoples as indispensable to restoring that relationship.

Meeting today’s ecological, social, economic and political crises demands the courage to move beyond familiar theories, policies and practices—to embrace different ways of knowing, deliberate across worldviews, and take seriously the ideas that are too often dismissed. In that sense, Indigenous political thought has much to offer for confronting these crises and reorienting governance. Yet no enduring transformation in governance is possible without first transforming how we understand ourselves, our responsibilities to others, and our place within the living world.

Ultimately, our common future will not be secured by material accumulation, economic growth or technological innovation alone. Nor will our emotional well-being and harmonious relationships with one another and nature depend on wealth. What is needed is the courage to imagine political possibilities that today may seem improbable. That requires asking deeper questions—questions Indigenous political thought has long posed: What separates us more than unites us? How do we wish to be remembered? What principles guide our actions? Where do we position ourselves in relation to other beings? As the Mundhum reminds us in the three sacred lines above: Life comes from the earth, dwells upon it briefly, and ultimately returns to where it began. How we choose to spend that brief time, however, is entirely up to us.

articles.title: AI renders analysis cheap, relationships expensive
articles.summary:
Last year I sat across from the managing partner of a small advisory firm while he named a fear most people in his seat keep to themselves. His partners are in their 70s and 80s. Almost all of the firm’s revenue runs through two individuals’ personal relationships. There is no real mechanism for anyone else to bring in work. He put it plainly: If one of them leaves, does the firm just crumble?

That question stayed with me for a year. Here is where it landed after around 125 conversations with owners and partners at small expert firms, and the advisors who work with them: In a world of AI, relationships matter more, not less. The cheaper the machines make everything else, the more the relationship becomes the thing a client is actually paying for.

Start with what AI is actually eating. The analyst layer. The research, the first-draft deck, the market map, the memo, the grind that junior people used to do and firms used to bill for. That work is getting cheap, fast. So what is a client still willing to pay a premium for?

Judgment, and the relationship that lets you apply it at the right moment. A senior partner at a large firm told me his firm has to move from 20 percent of its revenue coming from partner time to something closer to forty. And the forty, he said, is relationship management, influence, and turning insight into action. The part a machine will not do for you. The machine consumed the input. The human still owns the judgment and the timing.

We usually explain the rainmaker with the word charisma, as if it were a gift you are born with. I do not think that is right. The rainmaker’s real edge is discipline, and it is a discipline almost nobody else can afford to run by hand. Hold a live list of the people who matter. Notice when something changes in their world. Always show up with something worth saying.

Sounds simple. It is brutally manual. Someone who does this at a world-class level, professionally, told me each good touch costs him 15 to 20 minutes of research per person. His own word for it was annoying. And very manual. At another firm, the entire relationship history lives in about fifty spreadsheets, kept by hand, that break the moment a company belongs in two categories at once. The CRM they pay for is, in one partner’s words, no brain, just storage.

Run by hand, this discipline caps at what one head can hold. So the rest of the firm’s pipeline stays hostage to referral luck, and that is not a small thing. When I asked owners where their revenue actually comes from, almost none of them had to think about it. Somewhere between 70 and 90 percent came from referrals and warm relationships.

Going in, I assumed the complaint would get me more leads. It almost never did. Out of 40-odd firms, only a handful named leads as their first problem. What came up instead was quieter and scarier: The whole thing runs through one or two people, and no one has a plan for what happens when they stop.

Now put those two facts together. Analysis is getting cheap. The relationship discipline does not scale. Most people read that and conclude the machines win, and the human touch fades into nostalgia. I think they have it backwards.

When analysis was scarce and expensive, having smart analysts was a genuine moat. The relationship was one edge among several. Now that analysis is cheap, and everyone holds the same tools, the relationship discipline is close to the only thing left that a competitor cannot download.

A principal at one boutique put the contrast plainly: broad, generic outreach produces very few serious conversations, while timely outreach to the right person about something they actually care about performs materially better. Mass outreach is worth less precisely because it is cheap and easy to automate. Well-timed relevance is much harder to replicate.

There is a cruel twist inside this. The people who are best at the discipline are the ones with the least time to run it. A solo advisor said it better than any framework I have read: If you are working, you are not selling, and if you are selling, you are not working.

So here is the question I kept circling. If the rainmaker’s edge is a discipline and not a personality, can you turn it into a system that a whole firm runs?

I think you can. Not a personality you hire for, but an engine anyone in the firm can operate: Every key account gets watched, every key person inside it gets watched, and when something changes, whoever owns that relationship gets both the reason to reach out and the thing worth saying.

What that engine is really for became clear in one conversation. A principal wins the large majority of the engagements he actually gets in front of. His constraint is not closing. It is getting into more rooms, early enough to matter. The system is not there to replace him. It is there to get him more at-bats, earlier.

Zoom out, because the stakes are bigger than any one firm’s pipeline. There are tens of thousands of small expert firms, and right now they are squeezed from two sides at once. AI is eating the analyst work they used to bill for. And their growth engine, the rainmaker, does not scale and does not last. Going back to the room I opened with. Partners in their 70s and 80s. Revenue through two people. No way for anyone else to originate. That is not a rare firm. That is the shape of the whole category.

These firms have two futures. They grow past their rainmakers and outlive them. Or they die with them, or get absorbed by someone larger, because they never built a way to grow that did not depend on one or two people. That is the real choice in front of the category, and very few firms are making it on purpose.

The firms that make it through the next few years will not be the ones with the best analysis. Everyone will have that. It is already close to free. They will be the ones that took what their best rainmaker keeps in his head, knowing who matters and showing up at the right moment, and made it a system instead of a person. When analysis becomes cheap, relationship intelligence becomes one of the few durable advantages left. The firms best positioned for the next decade will be those that turn what their best rainmakers know into institutional memory that can outlast any one person.

articles.title: ‘Summer Love’ to be staged at Kantipur Theatre from Friday
articles.summary:
A stage adaptation of Subin Bhattarai’s popular novel ‘Summer Love’ is set to open at Kantipur Theatre, Gairidhara, Kathmandu, from Friday, August 14.

Produced by Kantipur Film Academy and directed by Samrat Bhujel, the play will be staged twice daily at 1:15 pm and 5:15 pm, except on Wednesdays. The production has a runtime of one hour and 45 minutes.

Actor and filmmaker Arpan Thapa is also part of the cast and will appear in the role of the writer from the novel. The actors portraying the story’s central characters, Atit and Saya, have not yet been revealed and are expected to be introduced during the premiere.

The production brings Bhattarai’s widely read romantic novel to the stage, allowing readers to see how the characters and scenes they imagined while reading the book have been interpreted through theatre.

The play marks another literary adaptation at the theatre, which previously staged a production based on Amar Neupane’s novel Seto Dharti.

“We are incredibly grateful for the love and support audiences showed ‘Seto Dharti’. We hope they will receive ‘Summer Love’ with the same warmth and enthusiasm,” said Samrat Bhujel, the director.

According to Kantipur Theatre, student tickets are priced at Rs300, regular tickets at Rs500 and special tickets at Rs1,000. Audiences have been encouraged to book tickets in advance due to limited seating.

articles.title: Sixty years of ‘Revolver’, the album which helped The Beatles push their limits
articles.summary:
Sixty years ago, the Beatles released Revolver, an album that has a strong claim to being the group’s magnum opus. Revolver’s 14 tracks represented an unprecedented and highly innovative kaleidoscope of musical styles at the time of release and laid bare what had become an insurmountable gap between the group’s live repertoire as it existed in mid-1966 and their increasingly lofty ambitions for their output as a recording group.

Consider that just a month prior to the album’s release, the Beatles toured Germany, Japan and the Philippines on the strength of a brief setlist that still included relatively simplistic songs like Chuck Berry’s “Rock and Roll Music” and Lennon-McCartney’s own “I Wanna Be Your Man” (given as a hand-me-down to the Rolling Stones three years prior). The Revolver sessions that took place immediately prior to this tour saw the band recording music that was worlds apart from what they were able – and still expected – to perform live, in what would prove to be the final days of their career as a live act.

Indeed, barely three weeks after the release of Revolver, the Beatles performed their final commercial concert at San Francisco’s Candlestick Park. Although the road-weariness brought on by years of relentless touring was the primary factor driving the group’s decision to call time on their career as live performers, they must have also taken account of the technological limitations of the era that prevented them from presenting their extremely inventive new music to live audiences.

With Revolver, the Beatles had entered their most intensively creative and experimental era and they would dedicate the remaining three-and-a-half years of their career as a group to being a full-time “studio band” bent on pushing the limits of recording technology to realise their artistic ambitions. Revolver is a timeless album, containing unforgettable songs, uniquely “fresh” production that manages to sound contemporary even today and an audacious artistic vision that is arguably yet to be bettered.

The following is a breakdown of the album.

George Harrison opened the album with an infectious rocker that belied an unexpectedly downbeat sentiment, the Beatles’ unhappiness at being taxed at a rate of 95% – yes, ninety five percent!! – of their earnings, a result of the then-recent election of Labour Prime Minister Harold Wilson (who is name-checked in the song alongside his Tory rival Edward Heath). The group’s unhappiness at the prevailing tax rate didn’t prevent them from continuing their relentless musical innovation, with Harrison using a 7#9 chord – the so-called “Hendrix chord” – months before it was popularised by Jimi Hendrix himself and Paul McCartney playing a coruscating guitar solo influenced by Indian classical music.

Eleanor Rigby

A total change of pace from the opening track, McCartney’s sparse, desolate, yet vivid ballad about a lonely old woman completely defied expectations of pop groups in 1966, both in its lyrical theme and its musical setting; surprisingly for such a poignant piece of music, the whole composition is built on just two chords! Producer George Martin’s expertise in producing classical music proved invaluable in bringing this track to life, with an innovative double string quartet arrangement featuring stark, staccato chords that echoed composer Bernard Hermann’s iconic score for Hitchcock’s Psycho.

I’m only sleeping

John Lennon’s first track on the album conjured up an enticingly languorous mood, with its passionate defence of the simple pleasure of lying in bed contrasted with the outside world’s mechanical tendency to bustle about – ultimately, to no great end.

“running everywhere at such a speed, till they find there’s no need”

However, such a sentiment did not prevent the Beatles from continuing to innovate musically and so they did with a guitar solo by Harrison recorded normally but played “backwards,” a technique that would become a staple of psychedelic rock.

Here, there and everywhere

One of multiple McCartney masterpieces on this record, this gorgeous ballad was written in surprisingly short order when the author arrived early one morning at Lennon’s home and had to wait for him to wake up. McCartney claimed to have been inspired by the Baroque form of the Beach Boys’ recently-released song “God Only Knows,” which he would himself later rate as the greatest song ever written, but he also drew from his own bag of songwriting tricks with the bridge sections featuring a masterfully executed modulation to G-minor, the parallel minor to the song’s home key of G-major.

Yellow submarine

The album’s designated “Ringo track” proved over the years to be a timeless classic with its evocative vision of a utopian shared existence on the titular vessel. This was also the first Beatles track unabashedly intended to be a “children’s song”; this, along with the sing-along “All Together Now” recorded the following year, hinted at a “return to childhood” theme that played an important part in the emerging counterculture.

Good day sunshine

The Beatles were as adept at absorbing outside musical influences as they were at influencing others, a point well illustrated by this McCartney track, which the author claimed was inspired by the sound of contemporary group The Lovin’ Spoonful and the microgenre of “sunshine pop” which they popularised (and which reached its zenith in 1966). A pure expression of McCartney’s musical personality, which exuded a relentless optimism and zest for life, this track also deftly incorporated many of his trademark songwriting tricks, including a syncopated chorus that is in a different key to the verses, and a startling key change in the outro.

And your bird can sing

An urgent, driving rocker, this enigmatic Lennon composition is among the album’s most memorable moments, and its cryptic lyrics have encouraged much speculation about who Lennon’s subject might have been (Frank Sinatra? Mick Jagger?). Although this track is rightly lauded for Lennon and Harrison’s technically complex twin-guitar lead line, an earlier attempt at the riff using only Harrison’s 12-string electric guitar may have been the better choice in retrospect; this version of the song was likely rejected by the group for sounding too much like The Byrds and was subsequently made available on The Beatles Anthology 2 and the “super deluxe” version of Revolver released in 2022.

Doctor Robert

This catchy Lennon track’s lively rhythm complements its narrative about a co-conspiring doctor who is not averse to supplying his patients drugs (not necessarily always of the prescription variety) that promise to “pick you up” and “make you a better man”, possibly inspired by a real-life acquaintance who enabled the group’s early experiments with LSD the previous year.

Got to get you into my life

Another upbeat McCartney track featuring an irrepressible, exuberant chorus, the Beatles decided to use a full horn section on this track, perhaps inspired by R&B music coming from American labels like Stax and Motown Records; this may have inspired a sub-genre of its own, as later rock groups like Chicago permanently incorporated a horn section into their own sound. McCartney’s aggressive side as a vocalist is on full display here, but the guitar solo appears to be a reheated version of the main riff from “Paperback Writer”, released as a single a few months prior.

Tomorrow never knows

One of the biggest leaps forward ever taken by the Beatles and one of Lennon’s unequivocal masterpieces, Revolver’s startling closing track was actually the very first track to be recorded for the album.

Although the title was taken from one of the malapropisms for which Ringo Starr had become notorious within the group, the lyrics were inspired by Lennon’s own explorations of eastern philosophy (in his case, of Tibetan rather than Indian origin) and the Beatles pulled out every sonic trick that the recording technology of the time could offer, including tape loops (a forerunner to modern sampling), another meticulously-constructed “backwards” guitar solo by Harrison and Lennon’s voice being fed through a Leslie rotating speaker – originally intended for use with Hammond organs – to give it an otherworldly nature.

To this day, “Tomorrow Never Knows” retains its power to astonish and mesmerise the listener; the pioneering recording techniques have held up surprisingly well over the decades, and still sound modern. Indeed, there is a good case to be made that, even sixty years later, “Tomorrow Never Knows” still sounds like the future.

This story was originally published in The Wire and is republished here with permission, under a special arrangement with The Wire.

articles.title: Exhibit review: How one trip to Banaras inspired nearly 20 different artistic visions
articles.summary:
‘HOMAGE TO BANARAS’, running at the Kathmandu Art Gallery, brings together close to twenty emerging Nepali artists from Lalitkala Campus, each of whom travelled to Varanasi, the sacred sister city of Kathmandu, on the same educational visit and returned with a different city entirely.

Walking through the Kathmandu Art Gallery’s rooms, the show reads less like a single-artist thesis and more like a chorus: portraits, ghats, boats, cremation grounds, and flame, all rendered by hands that had never touched Varanasi before and were changed by it anyway.

The gallery has arranged the work loosely by artist, where one gets to experience the works of students and alumni of Lalitkala and how they interact with each other when remembering their time in Varanasi.

To understand why so many artists converge on the same city with such different results, it helps to understand what Varanasi actually is. Sitting on the banks of the Ganges in northern India, Varanasi, also known as Kashi and Benares, is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and one of the holiest sites in Hinduism. Pilgrims travel there to bathe in the river, believing its waters purify the soul, and many Hindus consider it auspicious to die and be cremated there, since doing so is believed to grant liberation from the cycle of rebirth. That belief is made physically visible at Manikarnika Ghat, where funeral pyres burn without pause, day and night, in full public view.

A few steps away, daily life carries on around them: vendors, boatmen, worshippers, and tourists occupying the same narrow lanes and stone steps. Nowhere else does a city hold devotion and mortality this close together, in the open, as a matter of routine rather than an event.

That collision between the sacred and the ordinary is exactly what pulls the Lalitkala Campus artists towards Varanasi, and it's what the Kathmandu Art Gallery's exhibition design leans into. Arjun Basnet's work grew directly out of witnessing that collision at Manikarnika Ghat, where the continuous coexistence of cremation rituals and everyday life led him towards reflections on mortality and the fragile nature of existence.

Rather than depicting death itself, his pieces, including "Galactic Serenity-Souls" and the dry-point work "Witness to Ash I", use circular forms to represent imagined souls drifting through an infinite universe, carrying traces of memory beyond the physical body. He's careful to frame these forms as metaphors rather than literal depictions of an afterlife, images meant to invite contemplation of transformation and impermanence rather than illustrate them directly. Placed near the gallery's entrance, Basnet's work sets the emotional register for much of what follows.

Fire recurs across the show in a gentler form as well, in the nightly ritual of the Ganga Aarti, the fire ceremony performed on the ghats as an offering to the river. Bipran Chettri's "Ganga Aarati" traces back to witnessing the ceremony during a college study tour, an experience he describes as leaving a lasting impression through its rhythm, light, and devotion, and one that deepened his interest in symbolism and narrative.

Kajal Yadav arrives at the same ritual from a different angle: her paintings "Eternal Flame of Banaras" and "Breath of the Sacred" try to capture the glowing flame and rising smoke of the Aarti as an expression of what she calls the eternal flow of the Ganga. Hung together on the same gallery wall, Chettri's and Yadav's paintings let the Kathmandu Art Gallery stage a small conversation between two artists who never planned to be in dialogue, both reaching for the same flame from different distances.

Mukti Chalise, working in transparent watercolour washes of his own, produced ‘The Ganges’ and ‘Assi Ghat’ out of a broader interest in architecture, light, and atmosphere, moving beyond literal representation to capture what he calls the essence of a place. Pratibha Tiwari takes the river's traffic as her subject instead: her piece ‘Eyes adrift’ uses eye-shaped boats as silent observers drifting through the water, witnessing rituals, grief, prayer, and cremation without judgment, each boat’s eye painted a different colour to suggest that the city remains the same while every person who visits carries away a different Banaras.

The gallery has given ‘Eyes adrift’ its own sightline down the length of the room, letting its long, narrow canvas mimic the river it depicts.

Not every artist in the show is drawn to ritual or water. Some found their Varanasi in its architecture and its people instead, and the Kathmandu Art Gallery has grouped this work in a quieter side room. Henjilee Limbu, whose practice spans painting, writing, and music, found the city itself felt like a temple to her, not only in its ghats and shrines but in its withered architecture, narrow lanes, and forgotten windows, works she titled ‘Where the city watches’ as a way of recognising holiness in the ordinary.

Tshring Tamang, whose practice centres on portraiture as a way of studying human emotion and identity, found in Varanasi’s crowds and constant movement an unexpected sense of stillness, a discovery that reshaped how she understands both life and art, expressed in pieces like ‘Shanti’ and ‘Tyag’.

Prativa Khadka turned instead toward the city’s tradition of handmade crafts, captivated by its vibrant culture and history, producing ‘Treasure I hold’ and ‘Katha’ as reflections on the relationship between personal memory and cultural craftsmanship.

Perhaps the most literal engagement with the city’s material comes from Aayush Sunar, a sculpture student whose piece ‘Living and —’ attempts to hold Banaras in clay itself: the ghats, the crowds, the horizon of the Ganga stretching further than the eye can follow.

In his own description, the work’s form is restless, cutting in multiple directions and never settling into one, a shape he calls complex and unresolved, always mid-sentence. Below that restless form, the sculpture continues downward as its own distorted, dissolving reflection, an attempt to convey that what remains after complexity ends isn't peace, but only the echo of what was restless, disappearing into the shape of what we were. Given its scale and physical weight, the gallery has placed "Living and —" at the centre of its own room, the one sculptural anchor in a show otherwise built from paintings and works on paper.

That range, from fire and water to clay and portraiture, is really the story ‘HOMAGE TO BANARAS’ tells about contemporary art’s relationship to an ancient city, and it's a story the Kathmandu Art Gallery is well positioned to host. Varanasi has stood largely unchanged in its essential rituals for thousands of years: the same river, the same ghats, the same cremation fires burning continuously regardless of who is watching. What changes is the vocabulary each new generation brings to describe it.

A city whose meaning has traditionally been carried through oral tradition, temple architecture, and unbroken ritual practice is now being filtered through watercolour washes, fibre-resin casting, dry-point printmaking, and mixed media collage, media largely unavailable to the pilgrims and priests who shaped the city's original meaning.HOMAGE TO BANARAS

Where: Kathmandu Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, Kathmandu

Time: 11:00 am to 5:00 pm

Entry: Free

articles.title: Exhibit review: In ‘Dialogue and Perception’, colour does all the talking
articles.summary:
Some exhibitions ask viewers to search for meaning. Others ask them to surrender to feeling first. Sagar Manandhar’s latest exhibition ‘Dialogue and Perception (Sambad ra Dristikon)’ belongs firmly to the latter.

Stepping into the Kala Salon, what strikes first is not the subject matter but the remarkable harmony of colour. Every painting appears to revolve around a dominant hue, allowing secondary colours to grow organically around it. The canvases are saturated with vivid blues, oranges, yellows and purples, yet they never descend into visual noise. Instead, the colours settle into an unexpected balance, creating works that feel energetic without becoming chaotic.

The exhibition is unmistakably abstract, but abstraction here never feels directionless. Strong geometric forms anchor each composition while carefully maintained lines provide structure beneath the apparent spontaneity. There is discipline behind every gesture. Thin borders often frame the compositions, suggesting restraint, yet somewhere within each work a section seems determined to escape those boundaries, pushing outward as though the painting itself refuses confinement.

Walking through the exhibit, one begins to recognise a distinct visual language. Certain rhythmic squiggles recur throughout the paintings, resembling sound frequencies frozen into colour. They weave across the canvas like vibrations made visible, hinting that the artist experiences the world less through objects than through resonance. Even the sequencing of the paintings within the gallery feels intentional, almost as if viewers are moving through different movements of a musical composition.

It is difficult to mistake these paintings for anyone else’s. Despite experimenting with new techniques and materials, Manandhar has developed a recognisable signature. His brushwork, layered acrylic lines and rhythmic mark-making create a consistency that ties the exhibition together while still allowing individual works to explore different emotional territories.

Texture plays an equally important role. Paint bubbles emerge from the surface, thick acrylic ridges catch the light, while scratched lines and raised forms introduce a physicality that photographs cannot fully capture. In many works, the surface itself becomes part of the narrative. The acrylic seems alive, refusing to remain a passive medium.

Manandhar reinforces this relationship with material through his process. Rather than treating paint as something secondary to the final image, he describes acrylic as carrying emotion in itself. He speaks less about controlling an outcome than about trusting the process, allowing meanings to reveal themselves as he works. His abstraction is therefore not an attempt to conceal meaning but to discover it.

That philosophy becomes evident throughout the exhibition. These paintings do not feel planned in the conventional sense. Instead, they resemble emotional snapshots—moments where feeling has been translated into colour before language has the chance to intervene. There is something strangely nostalgic about them. Although entirely abstract, many of the works evoke the sensation of childhood, when the world seemed impossibly bright and uncomplicated. They feel less like representations of memory than the emotions memory leaves behind.

His understanding of colour further distinguishes the exhibition. Manandhar repeatedly places complementary colours alongside one another—blue against orange, yellow against purple—allowing contrasts to generate unexpected harmony. Colours that conventionally appear incompatible somehow coexist effortlessly under his hand. Small droplets of paint occasionally interrupt otherwise cohesive surfaces, momentarily pulling attention away from the composition before eventually folding back into it. Even these interruptions seem deliberate, preventing the eye from settling too comfortably.

Gradients soften transitions between otherwise bold passages, while the combination of acrylic paint and marker creates subtle shifts in texture and line quality. One senses an artist continually testing what his chosen medium is capable of.

Perhaps the exhibition's most compelling idea lies in Manandhar's relationship with sound. He speaks of having a special connection with auditory experience, something that manifests visually through repeated rhythmic forms and textured surfaces. Different scratches and lines remind him of different sounds produced by various materials. His experiments extend beyond canvas altogether.

Recent works include acrylic sheets that are allowed to dry into independent surfaces, as well as glass engravings that resonate like singing bowls when struck. These material explorations challenge the expectation that painting must remain confined to stretched canvas.

Interestingly, Manandhar says he sees paintings through palettes rather than individual colours. Rather than asking what blue or red symbolises, he considers what an entire palette feels like. This perspective explains one of the exhibition’s most intriguing inversions. While red is traditionally associated with anger, passion or heat, Manandhar instinctively reaches for blue. Likewise, sadness or emotional heaviness often emerges through reds instead of blues. The emotional vocabulary is deliberately reversed, forcing viewers to question their own assumptions about colour symbolism.

His influences also reveal themselves subtly. Manandhar credits his father, veteran artist Kiran Manandhar, as his greatest inspiration, particularly admiring his discipline and enduring creative energy. He also speaks of his appreciation for Buddha Nepali’s illusionistic abstraction. Yet despite these influences, the work never feels derivative. It remains distinctly his own.

The exhibition is not without moments of unevenness. Some experiments, particularly the detached acrylic surfaces, still feel exploratory rather than fully resolved. Similarly, a handful of colour droplets appear visually disconnected from the surrounding compositions, momentarily interrupting rather than enriching the rhythm.

Yet these minor imperfections seem inseparable from the exhibition’s central philosophy of experimentation. Manandhar is clearly less interested in polished certainty than in discovering what paint can become.

There is a temptation when viewing abstract art to search immediately for familiar forms—a landscape, a face or a tree. Manandhar acknowledges this instinct himself, observing that people naturally cling to what they already recognise. His paintings gently resist that impulse. Instead of offering identifiable subjects, they invite viewers to experience movement, rhythm, texture and colour before interpretation.

By the end of the exhibition, the paintings begin to feel less like images than recordings. They capture fleeting emotional frequencies that exist somewhere between sound, colour and memory.

‘Dialogue and Perception’ is an apt title because neither exists independently in Manandhar's work. The conversation begins with paint and canvas, but it doesn't end there. It continues between colour and sound, artist and viewer, certainty and imagination. His paintings ask for neither agreement nor interpretation. They ask only that we look– and perhaps, if we stay long enough, learn to listen.

____________________________________

Dialogue And Perception (Sambad ra Dristikon)

Where: The Kala Salon, Thamel

Time: 11:00 am to 8:00 pm

Entry: Free

articles.title: Two Nepalis killed on Romanian railway track
articles.summary:
Two Nepalis were killed after being hit by a train in Romania’s eastern city of Bacău early Sunday morning. Their identities have not yet been disclosed.

According to a statement from the Bacău Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (ISU), the two were struck by a train at around 3:21 am while walking along the railway line near Chimiei Street.

Emergency responders, including ambulances, rescue teams and medical personnel, reached the site shortly after receiving information about the incident. They found both individuals dead upon arrival, the ISU said.

Romanian police and railway authorities have launched an investigation into the accident.

“An investigation is underway to establish how they ended up on the railway line and the circumstances that led to the accident,” the ISU said in its statement.

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.

Around 60,000 Nepali students are currently enrolled in Australian institutions. Of them, about 56,000 are existing students, while roughly 4,000 are new arrivals.

Data from Australia’s Department of Home Affairs shows a sharp decline in new student arrivals from Nepal. Between January and May this year, only 2,700 of 7,500 offshore applicants from Nepal were granted visas. During the same period last year, 7,167 of 8,028 applicants received approvals.

The uncertainty surrounding visa approvals, combined with rising application costs, has discouraged many prospective students. Applicants currently have to pay an application fee of A$2,500 (approximately Rs260,000), which is non-refundable even if the visa is rejected.

Sanjeev Pandey, a Sydney-based lawyer, said Australia had welcomed a large number of international students after the Covid-19 pandemic, but authorities later became concerned about patterns of students changing courses and extending their stay without completing their original programmes.

“The government may have also tightened student visa rules to address growing employment and housing pressures,” Pandey said.

The stricter visa regime has raised concerns among education consultancies and smaller institutions that rely heavily on international enrolments.

Khagendra Satyal, international business development manager at Central Australian College, said the decline in student arrivals had significantly affected the sector.

“Visas are now granted only after assessing what positive contributions an international student can make to Australia in the long run,” Satyal said. “Students applying from Nepal need to understand this shift.”

The immigration crackdown also comes amid growing political pressure in Australia over migration. Analysts say the rise of politicians with hardline positions on immigration, including Pauline Hanson, has contributed to a broader political push for tighter controls.

Lawyer Pandey said the tougher environment has affected not only prospective students but also those already in Australia. Renewing student visas, switching back to student visas after completing post-study work arrangements, and bringing spouses as dependants have all become more difficult, he said.

Obtaining permanent residency has also become significantly more challenging compared with previous years.

Despite the tightening measures, Nepal remains one of the largest sources of international students in Australia. Government data shows Nepali students account for around nine percent of Australia's international student population, making Nepal the third-largest source country.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: म मेरो तर्कमा अडिग छु, सिंह दया र करुणाको प्रतीक होइन : हरि ढकाल
articles.summary:
सत्तारूढ दल राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा) का सांसद हरि ढकालले सिंह हिंस्रक, घमण्ड र शासककै प्रतीक भएको बताएका छन्।

articles.summary:
काठमाडौँ । नेपाल आदिवासी जनजाति पत्रकार महासंघ (फोनिज) काठमाडौँ जिल्ला कार्यसमितिको आयोजनामा वृक्षरोपण तथा फोनिज पदयात्रा सम्पन्न भएको छ ।

फोनिजको २७ औँ स्थापना दिवसको अवसर पारेर आज शनिवार काठमाडौँको साँखु–बज्रयोगिनी हुँदै मणिचूड दहसम्म पदयात्रा तथा विभिन्न गुम्बा तथा मन्दिर परिसरमा वृक्षरोपण गरेका हुन् । काठमाडौँ जिल्ला अन्तरगत फोनिज आवद्ध प्रतिनिधिहरू, स्थानीय जनप्रतिनिधि र विभिन्न जातिय संघसंस्थाका प्रतिनिधिहरूको उल्लेख्य सहभागितामा साँखुमा भेला भइ बज्रयोगिनी मन्दिर परिसरबाट करिव १७ किलोमिटिरको दूरीमा पदयात्रा गरेका थिए ।

पदयात्रापछि मणिचूड दहमा भएको औपचारिक कार्यक्रममा विभिन्न वक्ताहरूले धार्मिक पर्यटन प्रवद्र्धन र संरक्षणमा आदिवासी जनजातिहरूको महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका रहेको बताएका छन् । कार्यक्रममा बोल्दै शंकरापुर नगरपालिका वडा नं. ८ का अध्यक्ष पोते थिङले मणिचूड दहको महत्वबारे प्रकाश पार्दै प्रचारप्रसारको अभाव तथा राष्ट्रिय निकुञ्ज वन क्षेत्रको निश्चित मापदण्डका कारण अझै ओझेलमा परेको बताए । मणिचूड दह र त्यस क्षेत्रमा रहेका हरेक धार्मिक तथा साँस्कृतिक सम्पदाको संरक्षण र प्रवद्र्धनका साथै थप व्यवस्थापन गर्न वनसंग जोडिएको कानुनलाई परिमार्जण गर्नुपर्ने धारणा राखे ।

त्यस्तै शिवपुरी नागार्जुन राष्ट्रिय निकुञ्ज मध्यवर्ती क्षेत्र व्यवस्थापन समितिका अध्यक्ष श्यामकुमार वाइबाले निकुञ्जभित्र रहेको मणिचूड दह बौद्ध र हिन्दू दुवै धर्मालम्बीहरू पवित्र तिर्थस्थलको रूपमा मान्दै आएको बताए । विशेष गरि जनजातिजातिको बहुल्यता रहेको त्यस क्षेत्रमा बौद्ध धर्मालम्बीहरूले विभिन्न समयमा पूजापाठ, मोन्लाम लगायत साउन महिने जलयात्रा, जनैपूर्णिमा लगायत साँस्कृतिक पर्वहरू मनाउने भएकोले थप महत्व रहेको बताए । अहिले निकुञ्ज, स्थानीय तह र मन्दिर व्यवस्थापन समितिबीचको समन्वयमा व्यवस्थित बनाउने रणनीति रहेको बताए ।

कार्यक्रममा राष्ट्रि शहिद तथा शान्ति स्मारक पार्क र गोकर्ण यज्ञडोल सामुदायिक वन उपभोक्त समितिका अध्यक्ष सुर्दशन सिग्देलले वन, जंगल, जल र जमिनको संरक्षणमा जनजाति समुदायको उल्लेख्य भूमिका रहेको बताउँदै आफ्नो साँस्कृतिक पहिचान र अधिकारसँग जाडिएको क्षेत्रमा राज्यले दुःख दिन नहुने बताए । जनजाति समुदायले विशेष गरि प्रकृतिको पुजा गर्ने चाडपर्वलाई साँस्कृतिक पहिचानको रूपमा विश्वमाझ चिनाउन सफल रहेको बताउँदै राष्ट्रिय शहिद पार्क वन क्षेत्रमा समेत विभन्नि जातजातिको अस्तित्व समेट्ने गरि भिलेजग्रामको निर्माण गरिएको बताए ।

फोनिज बागमति प्रदेश समितिका महासचिव राजु नापितले फोनिजले पत्रकारितालाई आफ्नो पेसागत हकअधिकारमात्र नभएर भाषा, कला, संस्कृतिको संरक्षण र सम्वद्र्धनमा विशेष योगदान पु¥याउँदै आइरहेको बताए । फोनिज बागमति प्रदेशभित्र पत्रकारहरूलाई एकीकृत गराउँदै समुदायको पहिचान र अधिकार सुनिश्चित गराउन समेत जिल्लासमितिहरूले सक्रियतापूर्वक गतिविधि सञ्चालन गराउँदै आएको बताए ।

त्यस्तै फोनिज संघीय समितिका सचिव सुनिल महर्जनले फोनिज पदयात्राले रमाइलो मात्र नभइ अनुसन्धानका आयाम बुझ्न पाएको बताए । मणिचूडको सुन्दर ऐतिहासिक धार्मिक पर्यटकीय स्थल प्रकृतिप्रेमी र आध्यात्मिक शान्ति चाहनेहरूका लागि विशेष रहने बताउँदै पत्रकारिताको माध्यमबाट प्रचारप्रसारलाई तिब्रता दिनुपर्ने बताए । फोनिजले नेपालभित्र रहेका आदिवासी जनजाति समुदायसंग जोडिएका कला, भाषा, धर्म संस्कृति र पहिचान बोकेका विषयवस्तुहरूको अध्ययन र अनुसन्धान गरि विश्वसामु चिनाउने प्रयास गरिरहेको बताए ।

नेपाल आदिवासी जनजाति पत्रकार महासंघ (फोनिज) काठमाडौँ जिल्ला समितिका अध्यक्ष भिमबहादुर लामाले सामाजिक एकता र सद्भाव कायम उद्देश्यका साथ फोनिजको २७ औँ स्थापना दिवसलाई सार्थक पार्न पदयात्रा तथा वृक्षरोपण कार्यक्रमको आयोजना गरिएको बताए । उनले जनजाति पत्रकारहरूको पेसागत क्षमतालाई दरिलो बनाउन अध्ययन, अनुसन्धान र आलेख लेखनमा सहयोग पु¥याउने उद्देश्यले धार्मिक पर्यटकीय क्षेत्र तथा जनजाति समुदायको साँस्कृतिक तथा धार्मिक महत्व बोकेको क्षेत्र साँखु, बज्रयोगिनी र मणिचूड दहको यात्रा तय गरेको बताए । राज्य र पहुँचवाला समूहहरूबाट आदिवासी जनजातिहरूको थातथालोमा जलविद्युत गुरूयोजनाहरू सञ्चालन गर्ने, विकास निर्माण र राष्ट्रिय निकुञ्जको नाममा परिवारहरू विस्थापित बनाएको अध्यक्ष लामाले आरोप लगाए ।

फोनिज काठमाडौँ जिल्ला कार्यसमितिका सचिव रत्नमान महर्जनले सञ्चालन गरेको कार्यक्रममा नेपाल प्रहरीका पूर्व डिआइजी देउती गुरूङ, गोकर्णेश्वर नगरपालिका वडा नं. ८ का वडा सदस्य सुमन लामा, नेपाल पत्रकार महासंघ काठमाडौँ शाखा उपाध्यक्षद्वाय कमल राना मगर, कान्ति न्यौपाने, सहसचिब बिक्रम रत्न, मणिचूड मन्दिर व्यवस्थापन समितिका अध्यक्ष भिम घ्लान, नेपाल बौद्ध धर्म संरक्षण संघका महासचिव उमा गुरूङ, साँस्कृतिक युवा समूहका अध्यक्ष वेचन लामा, समाजसेवी किरण मोक्तान, सोफिया पाख्रिन लगायत अतिथि रहेका थिए । पदयात्रामा फोनिजकर्मी तथा विभिन्न संघसंस्थाका प्रतिनिधि गरि ६८ जनाको सहभागीता रहेको थियो ।

articles.title: Judicial Council to bar lawyers from direct appointment as Supreme Court justices
articles.summary:
The Judicial Council is preparing to prioritise career judges from the district and high courts for upcoming Supreme Court appointments, potentially ending the long-standing practice of appointing private legal practitioners directly to the top court.

According to sources within the council, preparations are underway to ensure that no lawyers in private practice are directly appointed to the Supreme Court in the upcoming round of appointments. The council is discussing whether to institutionalise a system in which judges with experience at the district and high courts are given preference for selection to the country’s highest court.

The appointment of Supreme Court justices has long been debated, drawing scrutiny from the public and the legal community. The Report on the Eradication of Malpractices and Anomalies in the Judiciary, 2021, prepared by then Supreme Court justice Hari Krishna Karki, identified deep-rooted problems in the judicial appointment process.

The report found that subjective, opaque and politically influenced considerations had often overshadowed the objective criteria set by the Constitution. It recommended that appointments be based on a comprehensive assessment of constitutionally qualified candidates, including their seniority, practical experience, knowledge of law and the constitution, efficiency, integrity, impartiality, professional and moral conduct, and contribution to the field of law and justice.

The report also pointed to nepotism, favouritism, political patronage and political quota-sharing among major parties, as factors influencing judicial appointments. In some cases, it found that individuals lacking the minimum qualifications required under the constitution and sufficient judicial experience had been recommended for appointment.

It is against this backdrop that the council has begun discussing a change in its approach to apex court appointments.

“To ensure that the persistent questions and allegations of political manoeuvring and partisan influence do not surface this time around, we are actively discussing the implementation of an appointment style that is distinctly different and more transparent than past practices,” a current member of the council said, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the deliberations.

The council member recalled an appointment made about seven years ago, when a large group of private legal practitioners were appointed directly as permanent justices of the Supreme Court.

After the appointments, a senior judicial colleague asked one of the newly appointed justices, who had come directly from the Bar, how he was finding the job.

“I am learning,” the justice replied, having spent barely a month on the top court bench, according to the council member.

“The Supreme Court is not a place to learn,” the senior justice responded.

The anecdote has resurfaced in the council’s current discussions over whether judges should first gain experience in the lower courts before reaching the apex court.

The debate has also been fuelled by questions raised over the performance of some justices appointed directly from private practice, including concerns about their efficiency, judicial temperament and overall performance.

There is currently no justice on the Supreme Court who has followed an uninterrupted career path from the district courts through the high courts to the apex court. The bench comprises justices appointed directly from private practice as well as those elevated from high courts.

The council believes the Supreme Court’s role as the country’s final court of appeal and a court of record, whose precedents bind lower courts, makes extensive judicial experience particularly important.

The council is chaired by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma. Its members are Sapana Pradhan Malla, the senior-most justice of the Supreme Court; Minister for Law, Justice, and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam; Mahesh Kumar Nepal, appointed on the recommendation of the prime minister; and Damodar Khadka, appointed on the recommendation of the Nepal Bar Association.

Asked about the forthcoming appointments, Chief Justice Sharma confirmed that preparations were under way but said the council had not reached any final decision on the candidates or their professional backgrounds.

He said the recommendations would be based on constitutional qualifications, experience and professional efficiency.

The proposed shift has already caused concern within the legal fraternity, particularly the Nepal Bar Association, which has long argued that appointments should include both experienced career judges and qualified lawyers from private practice.

Bijaya Prasad Mishra, president of the Nepal Bar Association (NBA), said the organisation had formally urged the council to maintain such a balance.

“We have explicitly told the Judicial Council and its chair to appoint judges of high integrity from both the ranks of career judges and the NBA,” Mishra said. “The NBA remains hopeful that this balanced approach will be followed. However, if this established practice is disregarded and the NBA is deliberately excluded, we will be forced to take a firm position against it.”

The constitution sets out several routes to appointment to the Supreme Court. Article 129 provides for up to 20 justices in addition to the Chief Justice. A person is eligible if they have served as a chief judge or judge of a high court for at least five years, or practised continuously as a senior advocate or advocate for at least 15 years.

The constitution also allows the appointment of someone who has worked continuously in the field of justice or law for at least 15 years and has gained a reputation as a distinguished jurist, or someone who has served in a gazetted first-class or higher post in the Judicial Service for at least 12 years.

The constitutional framework therefore does not exclude lawyers in private practice from the Supreme Court. The council, however, is considering giving priority to career judges for the current round of appointments.

The move comes as a shortage of judges has put growing pressure on the top court. Of the constitutionally prescribed 21 positions, including the Chief Justice, only 17 judges are currently active in regular hearings. Justice Til Prasad Shrestha has been away from the bench for an extended period while receiving cancer treatment in India, and a formal letter notifying him of his impending retirement has already been sent.

The remaining judges are dealing with about 25,000 pending cases, or roughly 1,470 cases per judge. Four positions at the apex court are currently vacant, a situation that has been exacerbated by the council’s practice of delaying appointments and leaving positions unfilled.

Chief Justice Sharma has acknowledged the problem. During his parliamentary confirmation hearing on May 19, he pledged to establish a system under which judicial appointments would be completed before vacancies occurred.

More than a month after his endorsement by the parliamentary hearing committee and appointment as Chief Justice, however, the formal process for appointing new judges had yet to begin.

Asked about the delay, Sharma said appointments at all levels of the judiciary would begin soon.

“The appointment of judges will take place soon. The council and I are making the necessary preparations,” he said. “The appointments will begin with the Supreme Court.”

The Judicial Council Act, 2016, sets out specific deadlines for appointments. Section 4 requires the council to recommend a Supreme Court justice at least one month before a position falls vacant because of mandatory retirement. If a vacancy occurs for another reason, the recommendation must be made within one month of the position becoming vacant.

Council has routinely failed to follow these deadlines. A council member, however, said there is now a push to comply with the statutory timeframe, beginning with the current appointments.

Nine High Court judges are currently being considered for the four vacant positions at the Supreme Court. The council is preparing a list of potential candidates that includes five current chief judges and other senior high court judges.

Those being considered include high court chief judges Rajan Prasad Bhattarai, Lal Bahadur Kunwar, Ratna Bahadur Bagchand, Hari Prasad Bhandari, and Rajeshwar Tiwari.

High court judges Dinesh Prasad Yadav, Krishna Lal Bhattarai, Yamuna Bhattarai, Tek Narayan Kunwar and Chandra Bahadur Saru are also being discussed. Yadav and Kunwar are serving as acting chief judges of the Dipayal and Janakpur High Courts, respectively, while Bhattarai is serving at the High Court, Dhankuta.

Appointments to the Supreme Court would, however, create further vacancies in the lower courts. The high courts currently have seven vacancies, including two chief judge positions and five judge positions. If four high court judges are elevated to the Supreme Court, the number of vacancies in the high courts would rise to 11.

The Constitution also sets eligibility criteria for high court chief judges. Candidates must have served as a district judge for at least five years or practised continuously as a senior advocate or advocate for at least 10 years. Those who have continuously worked in teaching, research or the practice of law and justice for at least 10 years are also eligible.

For district judge appointments, the Constitution requires a broader assessment of candidates. This includes their caseload, the extent to which their decisions have been upheld, quashed or reversed by higher courts, as well as seniority, academic qualifications and professional performance.

Candidates from outside the judicial service are to be assessed on the continuity of their professional practice, integrity, professional conduct and contributions to law and justice.

The debate over the current Supreme Court appointments therefore extends beyond the four vacancies. It could determine whether the council moves towards a more structured career-judge system, in which judges gain experience through the lower courts before reaching the apex court, or retains the existing practice of appointing lawyers directly from private practice.

articles.title: आज घट्यो सुनको मूल्य
articles.summary:
नेपाली बजारमा आज (सोमबार) सुनको मूल्यमा सामान्य गिरावट आएको छ। नेपाल सुनचाँदी व्यवसायी महासंघका अनुसार हिजोको तुलनामा आज सुनको भाउ घटेको हो।

महासंघका अनुसार आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतितोला तीन लाख एक हजार ५०० रुपैयाँ कायम भएको छ। हिजो (आइतबार) सुन प्रतितोला तीन लाख एक हजार ७०० रुपैयाँमा कारोबार भएको थियो। यसअनुसार आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतितोला २०० रुपैयाँले घटेको छ।

उता, आज चाँदीको मूल्य भने बढेको छ। आज चाँदी प्रतितोला चार हजार ६७० रुपैयाँमा कारोबार भइरहेको छ। हिजो चाँदी चार हजार ६४५ रुपैयाँ रहेको थियो। यसअनुसार आज चाँदीको मूल्य प्रतितोला २५ रुपैयाँले बढेको देखिन्छ।

अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सञ्चारमाध्यमहरूका अनुसार अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतिऔँस चार हजार ३२२ र चाँदीको मूल्य प्रतिऔँस ६३ अमेरिकी डलर कायम भएको छ।

articles.title: शीत भण्डार बनेपछि रत्नपुरका आलु उत्पादक किसान उत्साहित
articles.summary:
जिल्लाको चापाकोट नगरपालिका–८ रत्नपुरमा एक सय टन क्षमताको शीत भण्डार निर्माण भएको छ।

गण्डकी प्रदेश सरकार र चापाकोट नगरपालिकाको लागत साझेदारीमा रु एक करोड ६० लाखको लागतमा भण्डार निर्माण भएको हो। प्रारम्भमा दुई सय टनभन्दा बढी क्षमताको शीत भण्डार निर्माण गर्ने योजना रहे पनि बजेट अभावका कारण एक सय टन क्षमताको भण्डार निर्माण गरिएको चापाकोट–८ का वडाध्यक्ष टोपलाल न्यौपानेले जानकारी दिए।

विशेषगरी व्यावसायिकरूपमा आलु उत्पादन हुने रत्नपुरमा शीत भण्डार निर्माण भएपछि किसान उत्साहित भएका छन्। अब आलु भण्डारणका लागि भैरहवा, गल्याङको जिमुहा र पुतलीबजारसम्म पुग्नुपर्ने बाध्यता हटेको छ। एक बोरा आलु ती भण्डार केन्द्रमा पुर्याउँदा किसानले रु ५०० सम्म खर्च गर्नुपर्ने बाध्यात्मक परिस्थिति पनि अन्त्य भएको छ।

articles.title: राज्यले ठेकेदारलाई किन तिर्‍यो ११ करोड?
articles.summary:
दाङको घोराहीदेखि दक्षिण–पश्चिम रोल्पाको होलेरी, घर्तीगाउँ, थवाङ हुँदै पूर्वीरुकुमको हुकाम/मैकोट जोड्ने ‘सहिदमार्ग’ को यात्रा जोखिमपूर्ण छ।

सहिदका नाममा नामकरण गरिएको यो सडकले हिजोआज सहिदलाई नै गिज्याइरहे झैं लाग्छ। सहिदकै उपहास गरिरहेको दाङको घोराहीदेखि रुकुम जोड्ने उक्त एक सय ५१ किमिमध्ये धेरै स्थानमा मुस्किलले सवारी चल्छ। हालसम्म भौतिक प्रगति ५४ प्रतिशत र आर्थिक प्रगति ४० प्रतिशत भएको सहिद मार्ग सडक योजनाले बताए पनि स्थानीयले त्यसको अनुभूति गर्न पाएका छैनन्।

२०६४ सालदेखि हालसम्म सडक निर्माणतर्फ चार अर्ब ४९ करोड ५४ लाख ७३ हजार र पुलतर्फ ३४ करोड ४६ लाख ४८ हजार गरी चार अर्ब ८४ करोड एक लाख २१ हजार बढी रकम खर्चिए पनि गतिलो प्रगति भएको देखिँदैन। त्यसो त, दाङ घोराहीदेखि होलेरीसम्मको ३१ किमि पक्की सडक हस्तान्तरण नहुँदै पैदल हिँड्नसमेत जोखिम छ, तर सरोकारवाला मौन छन्।

कालोपत्र सडकको अधुरो कथा

३० नोभेम्बर २०१८ मा करिब ३६ करोड बढी रकम खर्चिएर दाङको घोराहीदेखि रोल्पाको होलेरीसम्म गरिएको ३१ किमि पक्की सडक हस्तान्तरण नहुँदै कच्चीभन्दा पनि कमजोर बनेको छ।

सहिद मार्गअन्र्तर्गतको उक्त ३१ किमि सडकमा मुस्किलले ६ किमि कालोपत्र बाँकी रहेको कर्मचारी आफैं स्वीकार गर्छन्। सिल प्यासेफिक जेभीले कालोपत्र गरेको भनिएको यो सडक बनाउने निर्माण व्यबसायीलाई राज्यले साढे ११ करोड रुपैयाँ उल्टै तिरेको छ।

कालोपत्र भएपछि करिब ९५ प्रतिशत काम सकिएको देखाउँदै सहिद मार्ग सडक आयोजनाले कार्य सम्पादन भन्दै रकम भुक्तानी गरेको थियो। १ डिसेम्बर २०१८ बाट लागु हुने गरी एक वर्षसम्म त्रुटि सच्याउने अवधि सुरु भयो, तर निर्माण व्यवसायीले बाँकी काम गरेनन् भने मर्मतमा पनि कुनै चासो दिएनन्। क्षमताभन्दा बढी भार बोकेर सिमेन्ट उद्योगका टिपर गुडेर सडक भत्किएको भन्दै निर्माण व्यवसायी काम नगरी बसे। त्रुटि सच्याउने अवधि ३० नोभेम्बर २०२१ सम्म पटकपटक गरेर दुई वर्ष थपियो।

बाँकी काम र मर्मतमा कुनै प्रगति नभएपछि २०७८ मंसिर ६ गते सडक विभागले निर्माण व्यवसायीलाई कालो सूचीमा राख्ने सिफारिससहित ठेक्का तोड्यो, तर यसअगाडि निर्माण व्यवसायीले न्यायिक निकाय ‘नेपाल मध्यस्थता परिषद् (नेप्का)’ मा उजुरी दिए। २०७८ भदौको अन्तिमतिर नेप्काले सडक आयोजनाले उल्टै निर्माण व्यवसायीलाई ११ करोड तिर्नुपर्ने निर्णय गरिदियो।

ठेक्का तोडेको सरकारी निकाय नेप्काको निर्णय चित्त नबुझेको भन्दै उच्च अदालत पाटन गए पनि अदालतले गत साल नेप्काकै निर्णय सदर गरिदियो। राज्यले निर्माण व्यवसायीलाई उल्टै ११ करोड तिर्नुपर्ने कारण न सहिदमार्ग सडक योजनासँग छ न त स्थानीयलाई केही जानकारी छ। निर्माण व्यवसायीले गतिलो काम गरेका थिएन भने उल्टै राज्यले त्यति ठुलो रकम किन तिर्‍यो ? क्षमताभन्दा बढी भार बोकेर सिमेन्ट उद्योगका टिपर गुडेर सडक भत्किएको हो भने राज्यले त्यतातिर किन ध्यान दिएन ? कमजोरी कसको थियो भन्नेबारेमा सबै मौन हुनु गम्भीर विषय हो।

११ करोड तिरेको स्वीकार गर्दै सहिद मार्ग सडक आयोजना प्रमुख माधवप्रसाद अधिकारीले नागरिकसँग भने, ‘हामीले न्यायालयले गरेको फैसला कार्यान्वयन गरेका हौं।’ उनले थपे, ‘उक्त रकम सोझै निर्माण व्यवसायीलाई नदिएर अदालतको धरौटी खातामा पठाएका हौं।’

एकपटक कालोपत्र गरिएको घोराही–होलेरी खण्डमा यतिबेला कालोपत्र गर्ने भन्दै सडक विभागले पुनः डिपिआर गरेको छ। माओवादीले सशस्त्र विद्रोह गरिरहेकै समयमा २०६० सालदेखि २०६२ सम्म देशका विभिन्न १३ जिल्लाका हजारौं व्यक्तिलाई यहाँ ल्याएर नुवागाउँदेखि थवाङसम्म श्रमदान गर्न लगाएको थियो। बाहिरी जिल्लाकाले १०/१० दिन श्रमदान गरे भने रोल्पालीले २०/२० दिन श्रमदान गरे।

उतिबेला १० हजार बढीले श्रमदान गरेका थिए। जिल्लामा गतिलो योजना भित्र्याउन नसक्ने रोल्पाली उच्च राजनीतिक नेतृत्वले दीर्घकालीन सोच नराख्दा यहाँका धेरै अन्य योजनामा सोचेजस्तो प्रगति हुन सकेको छैन। निर्माण व्यवसायीले राजनीतिक नेतृत्वलाई निर्वाचन खर्च गरिदिने गरेका कारण उनीहरूको विरोधमा कोही बोल्दैनन् भने कर्मचारीले केही गर्न खोजे उल्टै सरुवा पत्र थाप्नुपर्ने एक कर्मचारी बताउँछन्। ‘कर्मचारीले केही गर्न खोज्दा सरुवा पत्र आउँछ।’

articles.title: वीरगन्जबाट १६ ग्रामभन्दा बढी ब्राउन सुगरसहित भारतीय नागरिक पक्राउ
articles.summary:
पर्साको वीरगन्ज महानगरपालिका-१४ स्थित कृष्णा प्रणामी चोकबाट प्रहरीले ब्राउन सुगरसहित एक भारतीय नागरिकलाई पक्राउ गरेको छ। पक्राउ पर्नेमा भारतको मोतिहारी, पटोका श्रीपुर ग्राम पञ्चायत-१ बस्ने २५ वर्षीय शत्रुधन पासवान रहेका छन्।

प्रहरीका अनुसार आइतबार कृष्णा प्रणामी चोकस्थित सडकबाट उनलाई नियन्त्रणमा लिएर शरीर खानतलासी गर्दा १६.५७ ग्राम ब्राउन सुगरबरामद भएको हो। पासवानलाई नियन्त्रणमा लिएर घटनाबारे थप अनुसन्धान भइरहेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

articles.title: आज घट्यो सुनको मूल्य
articles.summary:
नेपाली बजारमा आज (सोमबार) सुनको मूल्यमा सामान्य गिरावट आएको छ। नेपाल सुनचाँदी व्यवसायी महासंघका अनुसार हिजोको तुलनामा आज सुनको भाउ घटेको हो।

महासंघका अनुसार आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतितोला तीन लाख एक हजार ५०० रुपैयाँ कायम भएको छ। हिजो (आइतबार) सुन प्रतितोला तीन लाख एक हजार ७०० रुपैयाँमा कारोबार भएको थियो। यसअनुसार आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतितोला २०० रुपैयाँले घटेको छ।

उता, आज चाँदीको मूल्य भने बढेको छ। आज चाँदी प्रतितोला चार हजार ६७० रुपैयाँमा कारोबार भइरहेको छ। हिजो चाँदी चार हजार ६४५ रुपैयाँ रहेको थियो। यसअनुसार आज चाँदीको मूल्य प्रतितोला २५ रुपैयाँले बढेको देखिन्छ।

अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सञ्चारमाध्यमहरूका अनुसार अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा आज सुनको मूल्य प्रतिऔँस चार हजार ३२२ र चाँदीको मूल्य प्रतिऔँस ६३ अमेरिकी डलर कायम भएको छ।

articles.title: खल्तीबाट डिजिटल भुक्तानी गर्दा दैनिक १ लाख र बम्परमा १० लाख जित्न सकिने
articles.summary:
काठमाडौँ । आईएमई खल्ती लिमिटेडले अर्थ मन्त्रालयअन्तर्गतको आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागद्वारा सञ्चालित ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम, २०८३’ मा आफ्ना प्रयोगकर्तालाई सहभागी गराउने भएको छ। खल्तीमार्फत रु १०० भन्दा बढीको योग्य डिजिटल भुक्तानी गर्दा ग्राहकहरू स्वतः दैनिक तथा पाक्षिक उपहार छनोटमा सहभागी हुनेछन्।

यस कार्यक्रमअन्तर्गत दैनिक एक जना विजेताले कर कट्टीपछि रु. १ लाख र प्रत्येक १५ दिनमा एक जना बम्पर विजेताले रु १० लाख प्राप्त गर्नेछन्। भुक्तानीको विवरण सुरक्षित रूपमा राजस्व विभागको प्रणालीमा पुग्ने र उपहार कुपन स्वतः सिर्जना भई खल्ती एपमै देखिने व्यवस्था मिलाइएको छ। विभागले प्रत्येक महिनाको १ र १६ गते स्वचालित प्रणालीबाट विजेता छनोट गरी एसएमएस, इमेल तथा खल्तीमार्फत जानकारी गराउनेछ।

बिलमा आधारित कारोबार प्रवर्द्धन गरी डिजिटल अर्थतन्त्र र राष्ट्रिय राजस्व प्रणालीलाई सुदृढ बनाउने लक्ष्यका साथ यो सहकार्य गरिएको आईएमई खल्तीका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत प्रवीण रेग्मीले बताएका छन्।

articles.title: सर्वसाधारणको रकम गरिमा विकास बैंकले झ्वाम पार्दै, झ्वाम पार्ने को–को ?
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । के तपाईंको गरिमा विकास बैंकमा खाता छ ?के तपाईंले आफुले मेहेनत गरेको रकम गरिमा बिकास बैंकमा राख्नु भएको छ ? यदी छ भने तपाईंका लागि आज दुखको खबर छ । कारण हो, ग्राहकले राखेको रकम बैंकको भवन किन्दा अपचलन गरेर प्रचलित मूल्यभन्दा बढी मूल्यामा किनिएको छ । प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदन र प्रचलित बजार मूल्यलाई समेत लत्याउँदै बैंक व्यवस्थापनले ३५ करोड ४० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी मूल्य तिरेको छ । सर्वसाधारणले दुःख गरेर बैंकमा जम्मा गरेको निक्षेप सुरक्षित छ त?भन्ने प्रश्न पनि उठिरहेको छ ।

गरिमा विकास बैंकले काठमाडौँको बालुवाटारमा ३७ आनाभन्दा बढी जग्गा र त्यसमा बनेको घर खरिद गर्दा प्रचलित बजार मूल्य र स्वयं प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदनलाई समेत लत्याउँदै करिब ३५ करोड ४० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी मूल्य तिरिएको भेटिएको छ। बजार मन्दीमा रहेका बेला प्राविधिक प्रतिवेदन भन्दा दोब्बर मूल्य हालेर जग्गा र भवन किनिएको छ ।

काठमाडौंको बालुवाटारमा कित्ता नम्बर ४९ मा रहेको २ रोपनी ५ आना १ पैसा अर्थात् ३७ दशमलव २६ आना जग्गा र ४७ हजार ६ सय २१ वर्गफिटको बनेको यो आरसीसी भवन शिखर इन्स्योरेन्सका पूर्वअध्यक्ष राजेन्द्रप्रसाद श्रेष्ठको २०८२ सालमा गरिमा विकास बैंकले केन्द्रीय कार्यालय बनाउन खरिद ग¥यो ।

बैंकले यो जग्गा खरिद गर्दा प्रतिआना १ करोड ५६ लाख १४ हजार ९२२ रुपैयाँ तिरेको देखिन्छ । अर्थात २ रोपनी ५ आना १ पैसाको जग्गाको मूल्या ५८ करोड १८ लाख १२ हजार रुपैयाँ बैकलाई पर्न गयो। अब यही जग्गामा रहेको यो भवनको क्षेत्रफल ४७ हजार ६ सय २१ वर्गफिट रहेको छ ।

बैंकले यो भवनको मूल्य ३९ करोड ३१ लाख ८८ हजार रुपैयाँमा खरिद गरेको देखिन्छ । वर्गफिटमा हिसाब गर्दा पनि प्रति वर्गफिट ८ हजार २ सय ५६ रुपैयाँमा खरिद गरको छ । तपाईलाई यो खरिद मूल्य सायद सामान्य नै लाग्यो होला? यो सामान्य घरजग्गा किनबेच देखिए तापनि, प्राविधिक प्रतिवेदन र बैंकको हालेको रकम जुधाउँदा भने ठूलो अन्तर देखिन्छ ।

प्राविधिक प्रतिवेदन र बजार मूल्यको वास्तविकता

पृथक इन्जिनियरिङ कन्सल्टेन्ट्सले बैंक धितोकै लागि तयार पारेको प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदन अनुसार सो क्षेत्रमा जग्गाको स्थानीय बजार दर प्रतिआना ८० लाख रुपैयाँ मात्र छ। स्थानीय व्यवसायीहरूका अनुसार पनि बजारको अधिकतम मूल्य ९० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी पर्दैन।

प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कन प्रतिवेदनमा सडकको अधिकार क्षेत्र कट्टा गरी कायम भएको १ रोपनी १३ आना ३ पैसा जग्गाको कुल बजार मूल्य १७ करोड ७० लाख ९८ हजार मात्रै कायम गरेको छ । पृथक इन्जिनियरिङ कन्सल्टेन्ट्सले कमर्सियल भ्यालु अनुसार मूल्याङ्कनको निष्कर्ष भनेको २३ करोड ८३ लाख ९९ हजार यो जग्गाको मूल्या कायम गरेको छ । फेयर मार्केट भ्यालु अनुसार मूल्याङ्कनको निष्कर्ष भनेको १७ करोड ७० लाख ९८ हजार कायम गर्यो ।

डिस्ट्रेस भ्यालु अनुसार मूल्याङ्कनको निष्कर्ष भने १४ करोड १६ लाख ७८ हजार कन्सल्टेन्ट्सले कायम गरेको छ । तर बंैकले बैंकले भने सोही जग्गालाई ५८ करोड १८ लाखभन्दा बढी भुक्तानी गर्यो। यो खेल जग्गामा मात्र रोकिएन, भवन खरिदमा पनि उस्तै अस्वाभाविक मूल्या हालियो ।

४७ हजार ६ सय २१ वर्गफिट क्षेत्रफल रहेको सो भवनको मूल्य बैंकले ३९ करोड ३१ लाख ८८ हजार रुपैयाँ तय गरेर खरिद ग¥यो। अर्थात् प्रतिवर्गफिट ८ हजार २ सय ५६ रुपैयाँ! निर्माण व्यवसायीहरूका अनुसार काठमाडौँमा अत्यन्त लक्जरियस सामग्री प्रयोग गर्दा पनि नयाँ भवन निर्माण खर्च प्रतिवर्गफिट अधिकतम ४ हजारदेखि ६ हजार रुपैयाँसम्म मात्र पुग्छ। प्रतिवर्गफिट ६ हजार नै मान्ने हो भने पनि २८ करोड ५७ लाख पर्ने भवनलाई बैंकले १० करोड ७४ लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी अतिरिक्त मूल्य हालेर किनेको देखिन्छ ।

जग्गामा २४ करोड ६५ लाख र घरमा १० करोड ७४ लाख गरी कुल ३५ करोड ४० लाख रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी रकम बजार मूल्य र प्राविधिक मूल्याङ्कनभन्दा बढी मूल्य हालिएको छ । घर–जग्गा बजारमा मन्दी छाएका बेला प्रचलित भाउभन्दा निकै माथि गएर गरिएको यो निर्णयमा गरिमा विकास बैंकका सञ्चालक अनिल रेग्मी, ईश्वरीप्रसाद ढकाल र सीईओ माधवप्रसाद उपाध्याय लगायतको भूमिका देखिन्छ ।

सर्वसाधारण निक्षेपकर्ताको पसिनाको कमाईमाथि बैंकका सञ्चालक र उच्च व्यवस्थापनबाट भएको यो अस्वाभाविक खर्चले बैंकको संस्थागत सुशासन र नियमनकारी निकाय नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकको अनुगमनमाथि ठूलो प्रश्न खडा गरेको छ।

articles.title: Prime Minister Shah breaks with self-imposed rule, meets Indian ambassador one-on-one
articles.summary:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Monday held his first one-on-one meeting with a Kathmandu-based foreign ambassador since taking office, ending a self-imposed rule of avoiding individual diplomatic engagements.

Shah met Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava at the Prime Minister’s Office in Singha Durbar. The meeting covered Nepal-India bilateral relations, mutual interests, development partnership and areas of cooperation, according to the prime minister’s secretariat.

Srivastava congratulated Shah and expressed his commitment to further strengthening relations and cooperation between the two countries.

Shah emphasised the need to deepen Nepal’s “historic relationship” with India and work together in areas of shared interest, his secretariat said.

The meeting comes as Shah has begun moving away from his earlier policy of avoiding one-on-one engagements with foreign ambassadors and senior visiting officials.

Shah is also scheduled to meet Chinese Ambassador Zhang Maoming separately on Monday, while US Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Scott Urbom is expected to meet him on Tuesday.

The decision to meet the ambassadors of Nepal’s two immediate neighbours on the same day appears intended to underscore their equal importance to Nepal, although the scheduling retains the government’s stated foreign policy priority of engaging India first, followed by China.

The meetings with the Indian and Chinese ambassadors were originally planned two weeks ago but were deferred following communal violence in Sunsari and other districts.

Since becoming prime minister on March 27, Shah had avoided individual meetings with Kathmandu-based ambassadors. Instead, he held joint meetings with foreign ambassadors on April 9 and May 26.

The approach was welcomed by some Nepali diplomats and foreign policy observers, who viewed group meetings as a more transparent and equitable way of engaging with Kathmandu’s diplomatic community.

Shah had also declined requests for meetings with several senior US officials visiting Nepal, including US Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Samir Paul Kapur and President Donald Trump’s special envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor. US Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah B. Rogers also did not meet the prime minister during her visit to Nepal.

articles.title: International Tibetan studies conference moved online
articles.summary:
The 17th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies, which the Nepal government instructed Kathmandu University to cancel, will now be held online, organisers said on Saturday.

In a statement, the International Association for Tibetan Studies (IATS) said Kathmandu University had been instructed by the government not to proceed with convening the week-long conference.

The instruction was delivered in person by Chief Secretary Govinda Bahadur Karkee and Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai to Kathmandu University Vice-Chancellor Rishikesh Wagle, Registrar Rajeev Shrestha and Sagar Sharma of the university’s Himalaya Centre for Asian Studies (HiCAS), according to the statement.

Karkee had summoned the KU officials to his office last Monday and urged them to cancel the programme, citing the sensitivity of the time and security concerns, according to officials.

Ahead of the cancellation, Chinese Ambassador Zhang Maoming held meetings with senior government officials and urged them to be cautious, according to government officials familiar with the matter. They said Chinese officials were concerned that pro-Tibet activists could use the conference as a platform for demonstrations.

Government and security officials said security agencies had also warned of possible demonstrations around the event venue and the risk of self-immolation by pro-Tibet activists. The concerns were conveyed to top government officials and some leaders of the Rastriya Swatantra Party, officials said.

A Western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, told the Post that Nepal’s decision to cancel the Tibetan studies conference, reportedly following pressure from Chinese officials, raises concerns about the impact of Beijing’s pressure on Nepal’s sovereignty.

“We hope Nepal will reverse this decision and allow Nepali citizens to exercise their freedom of expression and association,” the diplomat said.

The organisers had also written to Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel, warning that cancellation would have consequences for Tibetan and Himalayan studies and could damage Kathmandu University’s academic standing.

“It would be damaging to Kathmandu University, which would lose an important platform to showcase its strength and build new academic networks. It is also likely to cause reputational damage to Nepal through negative press coverage, and will have long-term repercussions in terms of economy, tourism, and academic collaborations,” said the letter, signed by Françoise Robin, acting president of the IATS, and Ulrike Roesler, secretary general of the IATS.

“The IATS Board cannot imagine that the cancellation of the conference can be in the interest of the Ministry of Education, which aims at fostering academic excellence,” the letter said.

The IATS board also sought the minister’s support to allow the conference to proceed, saying it needed immediate clarity on the status of the event because neither the board nor the convenors had received anything in writing from the government.
